Title: i went camping again--putz camping 2
Author: Victor D.
Article Content:
Last weekend, I went camping with my living group (Putz in East Campus) in Myles Standish State Forest, Southern Massachusetts. We went camping in early October last year, which was far too cold, overcast, and rainy. Moving our trip was definitely the right decision; warm enough even to take a swim in the pond!

would you consider this a meadow? when they told us we were going to a meadow this isn't what i imagined...
this is where we went swimming. i mean i didn't because i don't like the feeling of being wet outside of the water lol

Unfortunately, the area we went to didn’t have much elevation compared to last year when we submitted Monte Monadnock in New Hampshire. But our walk around the pond was nice. My friend and I were reminded of our walk around Walden Pond we did last semester, so we picked up our conversation on panpsychism from back then.

For what it’s worth, you may appreciate having talked about the transcendentalists in your high school English classes because I just can’t stop thinking about them whenever I’m near a small body of water anywhere in New England.

It’s always nice to get away from MIT and to have a day or two to be free of problem sets and “the grind”. Though come backing is always a struggle, and I’ve just barely caught up with my classes even though it’s been a week since camping.

I think I’ll miss these activities with my living group. This is my last time I’ll go on this camping trips with them, and I’ll miss the conversations that come up when we immerse ourselves in the forest.

Title: a love letter to McCormick--and thoughts on its renovation
Author: Hala K.
Article Content:
As I think about coming back for this school year,⁠01 I can’t help but realize that my daily routine will look a little different. When I step out of the Great Dome after classes, I’ll walk straight toward the Student Center instead of taking my usual left toward Maseeh. My amazon packages and doordash deliveries will need to be addressed to Vassar Street rather than Memorial Drive. Visiting most of my closest friends will no longer mean simply taking an elevator down a few floors but instead walking across Briggs field. And every time I walk down dorm row, I’ll have to walk past my favorite building on campus – with renovation signs staring back at me.

For the next 2 years, McCormick Hall – MIT’s only all-female residence – will be closing for renovation… and I’m devastated. It’s hard to put all of my thoughts in a single blog but this is an attempt at it:

some context on McCormick:

It’d be crazy to write a blog about McCormick without a quick history lesson. All of the information here is sourced from McCormick’s history page – extra shoutout to the amazing essay by alumni Tara Venkatadri included in this page. 

McCormick was started by Katharine McCormick in an effort to show that women belong in scientific fields and by extension, at MIT. In 1963, McCormick’s west tower⁠02 opened. By the next year, the number of female applicants to MIT had doubled. However, with the building filled to capacity, MIT’s administration argued that it would once again have to be more selective in admitting women because there was no longer sufficient housing for them. Katharine McCormick responded by providing another donation, leading to the opening of McCormick’s East Tower.

While I realize that some level of systemic gender inequality still exists at MIT – and, I’d argue, at any university – the opening of McCormick COMPLETELY changed what it looked like to be a woman here. And looking back at that history is crazy to me. 

My experience at MIT has never felt like a constant effort to prove myself against my male peers, nor have I felt that women feel forced to create a community among themselves in order to survive. Most of my classes, even the CS-focused ones, tend to have a pretty even gender split. And now, women can live in any MIT dorm they want. Some choose McCormick for women-only accommodations, others like the tight-knit community, and some were placed here by accident and fell in love with it.

my first impressions of McCormick:

My older sister is a former McCormick president and its number one cheerleader, so the decision to choose McCormick came pretty easily. Still, like most freshmen, I worried that I had made the wrong choice. 

That feeling lasted about five minutes into orientation.

I had barely started pulling my luggage out of my Uber when I heard someone yell, “KOMAIHA!” Confused, I looked up to see Raul and Flavia, McCormick’s Heads of House, waiting outside. They welcomed me like they had been expecting me all day, telling me how excited they were to have me, and how great the year was going to be. Then another car pulled up, and they immediately called out the next freshman’s name too.

I realized that they had memorized all of our names before we had even arrived. It seems like a small thing, but on a stressful day where everyone and everything is unfamiliar, being greeted by name means a lot. Looking back now, it was also a pretty fitting introduction to McCormick: a community that cares enough to dedicate a week memorizing photos of prefrosh just to make them feel at home on their first day. 

pre-frosh hala on move in day with Raul and Flavia 🥲
Previous
 
Next

McCormick community + staple events:

With only 255 residents, the second-smallest dorm after Random, McCormick is an extremely tight-knit community. I would guess that I’ve had at least one conversation with 80% of McCormick residents. And when I tell friends in other dorms that, they’re usually shocked. In a lot of dorms⁠03 , you become close with the people on your floor, plus a handful of others you meet at dinner or in the laundry room. I’ve never felt like those same “boundaries” exist at McCormick – in large part due to the fact that we don’t have floor culture, only dorm-wide culture. 

Though I think another reason for this is because of how many McCormick traditions bring the entire dorm together. There are basically unskippable⁠04 events happening almost every other week, organized by different chairs, presidents, and our AMAZING AMAZING AMAZING house team. At these events, you end up meeting a lot of people that live across every corner of the building. And over time, those repeated interactions make the whole building feel much smaller. Here are some of the most popular ones:

KARAO-CAKE! just like the name says, karaoke + cheesecake in the HOH apartment. easily the most iconic event ever.
BARBEQUE! this is an event held monthly by the McCormick house team + dining staff. amazing barbeque (that is 100% halal) and lots of fruits/desserts.
CHURRO DAY! another collab with house staff and McCormick dining. typical breakfast is replaced with homemade churros (THAT ARE TO DIE FOR) and sandwiches.
PASTA NIGHT! during IAP, most students opt out of a dining plan and cook for themselves. About once a week, McCormick runs a pasta making session where the entire dorm is invited to help cook or even just grab some pasta to go! i unfortunately don't have good pictures but these were leftovers from one day!
PIZZA NIGHT! (so many food based traditions) all residents are invited to make their own pizza with a HUGE variety of toppings in the HOHs brick oven. to this day, one of the best pizzas I've ever had
Previous
 
Next

But of course, the people are what make McCormick most special.⁠05 I talked about first impressions earlier, but the effort people put in on that first day to make you feel welcome stays consistent throughout your time here. Residents ask about your day in the elevator, GRAs remember your hometown and ask how moving in has been, and Raul and Flavia will invite you to sit with them at dinner just to hear about what you’re excited or worried about. During my first week at MIT, upperclassmen I had only briefly met while moving in invited me to join them for breakfast, probably realizing that I hadn’t made enough friends yet to have plans of my own. And somehow, it didn’t feel awkward or like I was butting in at ALL.

As someone who often felt homesick freshman year, this always reminded me that I had people here looking out for me too.

Another one of my favorite examples of that is McC-Fast, a weekly event held in McCormick’s Green Living Room. McCormick residents volunteer to tutor other residents, often freshmen, in classes they’ve already taken. For students whose schedules are already incredibly busy, choosing to spend two hours every week helping someone else is so selfless. During my first semester, my friends and I went almost every week for help with our 8.01 psets. Obviously, it helped me understand physics, but it also introduced me to other students in the dorm who later became close friends and pset buddies in completely different classes. I still haven’t heard of another dorm that runs anything quite like it.

Though my opinion alone might not mean much, so I asked some friends for words they associate with McCormick. They said wholesome, close-knit, toasty, girlhood, and slumber party. For me, the first word that comes to mind is homey. Maybe some of that is the slightly old-fashioned look of the building, but there’s something about McCormick that just feels comfortable the moment you walk in. 

thoughts on renovation

Visuals of how McCormick should look after renovations and specifics of what will be changed are shared here. 

Transparently, I worry that post-renovation McCormick will feel a little different. You know how time is divided into BC and AD? I’ve already started describing things as BR and AR: “before renovations” and “after renovations.” 

Some of the worry is purely derived from the physical changes. I can definitely admit that McCormick needs renovations, but I question if the “new look” will fit the dorm’s vibe. Will I still say that McCormick feels “comfortable the moment you walk in?” I remember seeing the proposed images for the new lobby and thinking that it looked a little too much like a hotel… like it was too polished.

That being said, student leadership has worked extensively with Housing and Residential Services to prioritize the things we really don’t want to lose. McCormick, for example, has these beautiful paintings scattered throughout the dorm, and a lot of them have been saved so they can go right back up AR. Students will be choosing the new furniture for the two main, communal living rooms. 

With that, most of my worry is actually about cultural preservation. Two years from now, I’ll be a senior, which means that by the time renovations are done, I’ll be one of very few residents who actually experienced both BR and AR. I feel some responsibility to make sure the traditions of McCormick and core cultural traits carry over. Enough so that the three classes of students who will move in having never lived there before still feel that same welcoming spirit I’ve kept coming back to throughout this blog. Enough so that they’re excited to show up for events, become part of the community, and eventually be the ones running those events for the next group of residents.

moving forward

Though with all of these concerns, I’m also REALLY excited. After renovations, I hope that the West Tower elevator will no longer randomly break, forcing me to walk up seven flights of stairs after an already long day. I hope the lighting fixtures are replaced so I don’t have to go to the bathroom anytime I want to see what my outfit looks like under non-yellow light. I hope that the game room projector actually works so I can watch Hamilton with friends without spending two hours fixing the machine first.

And in the meantime, McCormick won’t simply “disappear” for the next two years. House + student leadership have put in a lot of work to make sure there still exists women-only spaces like the ones McCormick used to provide, and that residents can still come together for the important traditions. 

Here are some of the really cool things they’ve already arranged for:

Tang Hall, a graduate residence, has allocated two floors for women-only housing for students who require or simply prefer to live only with women. McCormick’s area director also lives here as a supportive resource for undergrads living there. 
There’s a women-only gym in Tang with a huge variety of machines!
McCormick has its own lounge in the basement of Stud where current residents and interested future residents can study, hang out, and run events. Residents are actively working to make the space feel homier, but it already has a lot of things from our old craft room – like the 3D printer and sewing machine – plus furniture that used to be in McCormick.
McCormick dining used to be 100% halal, which was really nice for me as a Muslim student on campus. Because of that, Maseeh now has a halal dining section that only serves halal food and takes cross-contamination into account.
A lot of the iconic events I talked about earlier are coming back. McC-Fast, for example, now happens every Sunday and Wednesday from 7–9 PM in the McCormick Lounge (I HIGHLY RECOMMEND ANY FRESHMAN READING THIS TO ATTEND!!!), and Karao-cake is happening this week!

As I write this part of the blog, I’ve been living in New Vassar for a few weeks. I really like my room and a lot of the amenities here (AC, large lounge areas for each section, a good dining hall, etc.). New Vassar was also super accommodating to displaced McCormick residents and created a women-only section for us. That means a lot of my neighbors are former McCormick residents and familiar faces.

But I think, in a lot of ways, this blog has already proved itself right: I really do miss McCormick. My friends and I wanted different things from housing this year, so we mostly split between Tang, New Vassar, and Simmons. Now, seeing each other takes more effort. I don’t just happen to run into someone at dinner or walk downstairs and find half my friends sitting in the same room.

So yes, I’m excited to move back into McCormick AR. I hope the building feels newer, but that the parts that made me fall in love with it still feel exactly the same. And I hope that, after reading all of this, you’ve fallen a little in love with McCormick too. If you end up at MIT or already go here, I hope that I’ll get to welcome you as a future neighbor and scream Taylor Swift with you at Karao-cake.

Title: good things come to those who wait--being greedy on facebook marketplace
Author: Taylor L.
Article Content:
When my roommate flew back home after finals at the end of the spring semester, she bequeathed her bike to me until she returned, which was about a week. I was hanging around to volunteer with the MIT EMS medical detail for graduation and start my UROP, so I figured that I would try cycling around for a change. 

Nothing would ever be the same.⁠01 I always swore off bikes and scooters because I figured that my legs work fine for walking. That’s true, but I never realized how much it truly annoyed me to have to budget fifteen minutes to walk to class. Chipotle and Cava were now five minutes away instead of twenty. Graduation was happening on Killian Court, and I could literally leave three-ish minutes before I was supposed to be there. Getting a bike unlocked levels of lazy and last-minuteness I’d never even dreamed of before. 

When my roommate returned, I was devastated when she took back her bike because it meant I would have to walk across the bridge every morning to get to lab and every evening to get back to the frat in Boston we were staying at. I did that for two days before I snapped. I was getting so many steps in, at the cost of my sanity. One of the best parts of UROPing is that you can get paid, and so I set out to buy my own bike with my newfound exorbitant wealth.⁠02  

I ventured into the wilderness of Facebook Marketplace looking for my perfect bike, so much so that I added scrolling Marketplace into my social media rotation. I developed this plan where I would Bluebike to the seller’s house and hopefully ride my shiny new bike back. This failed three times before it succeeded because I failed to realize that there are different sizes of road bikes. I think the worst time was when I went up to Somerville to look at a gorgeous pink Cannondale while it was raining, and it didn’t work out because it was too tall.⁠03 I had to Bluebike back in the rain, which had only started pouring more. It seriously felt like the ride of shame.  

I eventually ended up with a nice Bianchi, and it was a 10/10 life-altering purchase. I made a rule for myself during my UROP that I absolutely had to leave the lab during lunch and go outside and get sunshine, and with the bike I had enough time to go back home and cook a nice little lunch. I had amazing work-life balance. 

The bike infrastructure in Boston could use some work, but I’m honestly happy that there’s bike lanes at all, because in Winston-Salem you just have to ride in the main lane and hope nobody hits you. It’s super developed around campus, and riding along Mass Ave makes me feel so cosmopolitan. I figured I should go for some longer rides at some point as well. There’s a great-ish bike path right next to campus that runs along the Charles River, on both the Cambridge and Boston side. I would recommend, but I did get lost a few times, which is impressive considering it’s mostly a straight path. There’s also a lovely area up north in Somerville called Mystic Lake that I learned about after kayaking there, with some peaceful viewing spots and a little beach. 

A picture from Mystic Lake. Kind of looks like a New England postcard
Shannon Beach! Surprisingly nice for a beach that's on a lake
The Tufts Sailing Pavilion is actually here as well. Super cool but I never saw any boats launch.

I never stopped scrolling, and at this point I was hooked on Marketplace and wanted to spend more money. I honed in on my next target, and, after some digging, I found a surf green Fender Stratocaster for $100. The seller even threw in a mini amplifier for free. I rode to their house on the bike and rode back through Fenway with the guitar case on my back, and I felt like I’d really mastered Marketplace. 

Learning guitar was about the only useful thing I did during the COVID lockdown, but in my freshman year, I barely even thought about it. My dorm has a music room down in the basement, but it was always a bit of an event to get there and play, because I’d have to walk all the way down six floors and get the key from the front desk. I probably practiced about twice the entire year, but now I have it on a stand next to my bed, and I can just pick it up and play a bit for five minutes before or between some homework. It’s truly one of the best quality of life improvements I’ve made. 

The love of my life

So here’s the issue I’m running into here: I’m too good at finding exactly what I want on Marketplace eventually, but how long am I willing to wait until the “perfect” thing falls into my lap? For my bike it was three weeks, and I spent those three weeks walking/busing/Bluebiking. It was inconvenient, of course, but I can consider that period of inconvenience as part of the price for finding a bike that I love now. For my guitar it was more like a week, but I passed on about one hundred other ones during that span because they weren’t speaking to me. 

Us economists⁠04 like to think of choices like these in terms of opportunity cost, which is the value of the next best option that you had to forgo to make the choice you did. If you pick A, then your opportunity cost was the value you would have gotten from B. If A costs $10 and gives you 5 imaginary units of happiness, and B costs $8 and gives you 3 units of happiness, then the opportunity cost of picking A is B and the $2 that would have been in your pocket if you’d bought B.

I’ve written before about being indecisive, and I’m finding new metaphors to articulate it here. In a perfect world where everybody behaves perfectly rational and in their own best interest, every choice would be made to minimize opportunity cost and maximize benefit—in other words, to get the most value while giving up the least. I think sometimes I get too caught up in the idea that what I have now or what’s in front of me is good, but there could be something better that I don’t even know about yet. And I always wonder whether I should stand there and welcome it when it finally comes, if it does come, or whether I should take a good thing for what it is and move on.

Here’s another example: During the spring semester, I had a 9am that I would be consistently late to because I’d go to the Z before it.⁠05 To cut some dead weight and shave a few seconds off my commute, I decided that I would just leave my gym duffle in a locker during the day and come pick it up in the afternoon or evening once I was done with classes. 

The Z closes at 11, so whenever I was too sleepy to go fetch my bag, I played a game I call locker roulette. Every night, the Z staff are supposed to comb through the locker rooms and cut locks if they’re left on, and also empty out lockers if people leave stuff inside of them. There’s a lot of lockers, though, and sometimes you can get away with leaving your stuff there for one night, if you’re lucky. 

So, when I neglected to collect my bag by the end of the day, I would come to check on it in the morning with great fear in my heart. I could only figure out the state of my belongings once I said a prayer and opened the locker.⁠06 I played this game pretty often and usually I won, but they got me twice. The first time, they cut my lock, which was actually a little upsetting because I’d had the lock for years, and the combination was 10-20-30, which was really easy for me to remember. The second time, I hadn’t bothered to buy another lock, so they just took my stuff. Each time they held my bag for ransom at the front desk until I gave them $10, so this ran me a total of $20. 

Let’s run the math here. Students can rent lockers for $4/month. I didn’t buy a locker until May, so I didn’t have to pay that eight months worth of rent, which is $32. I only ended up paying $20 in fees. So I saved $12. 

It gets better. There’s two women’s locker rooms in the Z. One is located in the depths after you scurry through a few hallways, and one is near the pool, and it’s objectively better in my opinion. I’d been looking into renting a locker earlier, but only the ones I didn’t want were available then. Then on one beautiful spring day in May, I checked the website and there were pool lockers available. So not only did I save $12, but I also ended up with a better locker. 

I think it’d be interesting to weigh the pros and cons of my purchases through the economists’ lens, and try to figure out if I’d been silly and accidentally chosen the second-best option instead of the first. But maybe I’d be too analytical trying to make everything so quantitative, because whatever units of happiness I choose are imaginary and we’re really just guessing as to whether buying a green or a red guitar maximizes my benefit. Let’s say instead that shopping comes from the heart. What if I just take the best thing I see in front of me?

Let’s pretend that when I open Facebook Marketplace I become a greedy algorithm, which you code to try and solve a problem with constraints (like a budget or a time frame). It navigates through combinations of resources in a certain way, depending on how you program it, and spits out the first viable solution it finds. Oftentimes this isn’t the most efficient solution, but if you’re only looking for something that works, it’s fine. So maybe I decide that I want my guitar now, and I don’t want to wait for any other listings, so I’m just going to buy the one I like the most out of what’s on my screen.

The two options here are overthinking and underthinking, and I don’t really want to do either of those, but there are too many roads that lead back there. A lot of the time I find myself considering a bunch of what-ifs, which is a little weird to me because I’m very happy with where I’m at, but something in is me always wondering if I’ve made a wrong decision at some point that’s kept me from ascending and reaching nirvana. Maybe I was too hasty and sprung for something I shouldn’t have; maybe there was a better, cheaper bike posted a day after I bought mine, but I’ll never see it because I pulled the trigger already.

Title: HUGE dormspam haul!!! 😱😱--on trust, community, and a cry for help
Author: Suzuko O.
Article Content:
WELCOME BACK GUYS TODAY WE ARE GOING TO BE GOING THROUGH MY DORMSPAM HAUL! OVER THE PAST TWO WEEKS I’VE BOUGHT A LOT OF FUN STUFF SO MAKE SURE TO READ TILL THE END!

yeah i do not really have any platform where i watch shortform video so i don’t really know how hauls usually go. but i thought this was a fitting format for what i want to talk about

every fall, mit students’ inboxes start to fill: first with a trickle of announcements (“come to caving club’s first meeting this tuesday”), which then becomes a deluge (“interested in sloan business club?” “chess club has boba 5:30pm friday!” “want to help plan mit science olympiad?”). it’s almost magical. how is it that all of these messages find their way to my email, ready for me to peruse during chem class?⁠01

dormspam!

dormspam is a campus-wide mailing list⁠02 used as a sort of universal message board. anyone can send letters about anything: besides club announcements, i’ve seen dormspams asking me if i want to buy ed sheeran tickets (not really), soliciting me to participate in some medical survey, announcing a lost glasses chain, reminding people from one of 8 states (including california!) to vote, and advertising a “senior sale”. this is a wonderfully diverse array of messages; today, i want to focus on the last genre – THE SALES!

for context, i lean pretty anti-consumerist. this is mostly from an environmental standpoint⁠03 – i think most people buy more stuff than they actually need, and i especially think cheap clothes are just not worth it. but dormspam gives me the thrill of buying cheap stuff without the guilt! which is great and also which is why i get a slightly concerning burst of energy whenever i see a new “sale!” slide its way into my outlook. 

what i bought

i’ll go in chronological order for all of my purchases.

1. bike helmet ($3)

mit (and cambridge/boston in general) has a reasonably high number of people who rely on bikes to get around, especially among those who have a low tolerance for walking. i personally do not own a bike but want to have the option of being able to bike – for example, if i want to take a bluebike.⁠04 (UPDATE after i wrote this part of the blog i did in fact spend a day bluebiking around! i went to allston to get lunch, then to harvard, then back to mit)

see the lamp too! also the print i borrowed from the list art center! also the big shark! ignore my messy desk!

you’ll see tons of people riding around campus without a helmet. why, you might ask, did you go out of your way to walk to an off-campus apartment to pay a stranger three dollars to wear a strange hat on your head? 

the reason is because evan, a fellow tetazoan, got hit by a car this summer while biking, breaking his leg⁠05 and cutting up his face. according to him:

helmets are the only reason you see me caned up instead coma-d up. Cars in Cambridge are crazy

so yes, psa: wear a helmet while you bike! your friends and family will thank you.

2. two lamps ($5) 

immediately after moving into my temporary room, i realized the necessity of smaller lights. each room only has one light on the ceiling, and the light switch is located at the door, which makes it annoying if you want to lay in bed with light to relax but then you have to get up and turn the light off before you can actually sleep. 

i initially considered buying a lamp from mujirushi or something before fpops,⁠06 but the only option they had was like $75, and i did not think this was worth it. it turns out that this was a good decision because i was able to purchase these two lamps for $5! 

when i picked them up from the food delivery desk in east campus, i immediately realized that they were like significantly larger than i expected them to be – like maybe twice the length scale? their blinds are a little dirty, as advertised, and the lightbulbs seem to be incandescent⁠07 instead of led or fluorescent, but they function very well and i think two lamps for $5 is a much better deal than $75 for one. yippee!

he longs to escape

3. 100 feet of rope ($0.50)

i mostly bought this for the funnies. this was on the same sale as the one where i bought the lamps, which was somewhat unique in that it was run as an auction instead of having a list of set prices. one of the items was listed as ~100 feet of rope (“I dont know how much exactly, its a lot though”) and i saw it and was like I MUST PURCHASE THIS

so i bought it for 50 cents. yeah uhh not sure what i am going to do with my approximate one hundred feet of black rope but surely i must eventually be able to find a use for it right??

yeah idk what i can do with this

4. winter boots ($8)

clothes are a bit harder to buy on dormspam because sizing is very hit or miss. also i feel like on average the people who sell clothes on dormspam tend to lean fem? which does not align with how i typically like to dress. but in this case it works out!

these boots are a womens’ 9, which corresponds to a mens’ 7.5, which i immediately recognized as being my shoe size and therefore quite a good investment. being from la, i did not really own a pair of winter shoes (what do you mean there is FROZEN WATER on the roads ??) and i am very glad that i can get a pair for under ten dollars instead of like a hundred or whatever shoes cost. i think these boots are a smidge smaller than i would prefer but it should be fine? hopefully

very solid

these i had to pick up from burton-conner⁠08 this was a nice excuse to visit friends! :D also a good way to get myself to walk outside instead of rotting⁠09

5. winter jacket ($35)

WOAH you might think. that is rather pricey compared to the other objects on this list! THIRTY FIVE whole dollars? on dormspam?

well, i am actually wearing this jacket right now as i write this⁠10 and i still think this was a worthwhile purchase. it’s in a nice brown that i like, it is quite warm, and it fits me almost perfectly. luckily i was able to try on for size before i bought it – i did this in the lobby of graduate junction, one of the grad dorms, where i verified that it fit and then sent away 35 dollars of my hard earned cash. it’s quite warm and makes me feel very cool. good purchase!

alejandro sniped me WTF

it’s already starting to be pretty cold here,⁠11 especially at night, so i’m glad i have more clothing options. yeah considering this jacket retails for i think around a hundred dollars i am very happy with this. 

6. eyeliner ($5)

this was definitely the most frivolous purchase on this list – someone was selling a bunch of their random crap for under ten dollars, and this was being sold as an unused eyeliner pencil for five dollars. i debated whether it was worth it but eventually decided to get it. 

i did zero makeup in high school and have been doing near zero makeup here, but i bought this because i want to have the option to express myself more dramatically on special occasions. not sure. maybe halloween? maybe reawakening?⁠12 lots of exciting possibilities. 

it is remarkably waterproof. how do they do that?

so that concludes the haul part of this post! as you can see i have derived a lot of enjoyment from buying random stuff. the joys of consumption : ) now we transition to what i think these dormspam sales represent about what i like about mit:

dormspam is about trust

when we, as mit students, subscribe to dormspam, we do it because we trust our peers. we trust that the messages we get were sent by someone who believes that the words they write merit the collective hours of time that we, the mit community, spend reading their words. 

this trust is enforced in part by the norms of dormspam.⁠13 senders must tag their email “bcc’ed to dorms” or risk wider castigation; senders must, too, broadcast their underwear color as a promise of their vulnerability⁠14

this trust, too, is what allows my boundless consumption to flourish. it is my trust that after i send five dollars and fifty cents to someone named max, that this faceless person will leave two surprisingly-large lamps and a long tangle of black rope on the food delivery table in east campus. it is my trust that after walking twenty-five minutes all the way across campus to grad junction, a dorm filled with twenty-five year old REAL ADULTS, an email address becomes a person passing on the warmth of her jacket to an ingénu from her city. mit’s culture of trust keeps items out of the trash and keeps me out of debt. 

i guess the metaphor is that these items that i buy represent institutional knowledge, like the wisdom that these upperclassmen have reaped over their years here. for my part, i trust the institutional knowledge. for theirs, they trust the idea that institutional knowledge is something that should exist, and that should continue, and they do their part to propagate this.

dormspam is dying… but we can save it 

up until two years ago, dormspam was opt-out: all mit first-years would be immediately enrolled, removed only if they both really didn’t want to be on it and also got over the activation energy hump to intentionally get themselves off the list⁠15

but in september 2024 this changed. now dormspam is opt-in, and the heft of inertia is against us. now, before freshmen can get access to the vast trove of information that is dormspam, they first have to open a few tabs, clicking around and typing, setting up a filter so that everything goes neatly in its own folder;⁠16 but this can only happen given that our freshman already knows of dormspam’s existence and understands its significance. a high bar! so many times have i told a friend “oh yeah i bought this off dormspam” only to hear “oh i didn’t know dormspam had sales i’m not on it yet”

lacking new blood, dormspam is at risk. dormspam only lives so long as people animate it – with their club announcements, their autumn sales, their flame wars. if fewer and fewer freshmen join dormspam every year, it’s not far-fetched to imagine a future fully dormspam-less. people will speak in the past tense about: “wow, i was scrolling through the archives and look at this funny random survey i found!” like latin, dormspam will calcify. 

this would be a tragedy!

i know this, but i’ve only been here a month. ultimately i just do not have enough experience to express just how sad this would be, so here are some words from other people

in the words of petey, our well-aged Blog Dad:

Dormspam is a unique form of campus-wide communication that I haven’t really seen anything else like at any other school

more emphatically, the borrowed words of fellow blogger allison ‘28:

I think, as much as MIT seems like a monolith of Nerd from the outside, the undergrad experience here can be a somewhat fragmented landscape. Between our different majors and different living groups and different student orgs, a lot of our lives orbit completely disjoint sets of experiences. 

It’s one of the best things about MIT, that you can find your niche and your people and do amazing things with them. But it also means at a school with thousands of undergrads, it’s difficult to have shared experiences.

Dormspam is the one thing that crosses most of those lines.

We all see the bicycle sale flame wars, or the 5W toilet picture, or the random number survey. It’s something you can bring up that many people across MIT will know about. We share the experience of being inundated with 200 senior sales in the last week of classes. 

THE COMMUNAL THOUGHT CLOUD OF THE MIT STUDENT BODY MUST LIVE ON. What else would we use for our entertainment? For sustaining our free food needs? For selling our unwanted belongings and sharing our advice and coordinating massive campus-wide projects?

so what can we do?

well, if you happen to be a mit freshman, MAKE SURE YOU ARE ON DORMSPAM. i promise it’s easy and it is SO worth it. go to https://sites.mit.edu/how-to-dormspam/unsubscribe/; this website has a list of dormspam mailing lists for all dorms! just click the link next to the list that matches your dorm! for example if you live in simmons you would click this link:

it’s called that because simmons looks like a sponge (look it up!)

this website also contains very useful information about filtering dormspam so that your main inbox doesn’t get clogged. 

if you are already on dormspam: GET YOUR FRIENDS ON DORMSPAM GET EVERY SINGLE OTHER FROSH YOU KNOW ON DORMSPAM THEY (AND I) WILL THANK YOU. also, learn to send dormspams! find something that you actually think is worth sending to all of mit, and then send a message as described here: https://sites.mit.edu/how-to-dormspam/send/ (i actually haven’t done this yet so maybe i can’t say anything)

if you are older than a mit freshman: the above instructions still hold but less emphatically. actually i guess if you are an upperclassman MAKE SURE YOUR FROSH ARE ON DORMSPAM

if you are younger than a mit freshman: unfortunately the joys of dormspam sales are not yet for you. but they await you in the wide, beckoning future. so if you do end up here, keep dormspam in your mind. and if you find yourself in some evil world where dormspam has died, perhaps you (yes, you, dear reader) can be the one to resurrect it. 

the nature of material possession is to fade. i know my dormspam sale finds are not meant to last. but if nothing else, i hope the backbone behind dormspam lives forever, built off its foundation of trust and community.

Title: Beaches and Bioreactors--summer is gone and I'm trying to move on
Author: Nicholas R.
Article Content:
We’re over two weeks into the school year now, yet my brain has hardly registered the fact that summer is over. Following all the hustle of Orientation⁠01 , rush week⁠02 , and the end of my UROP, the start of classes felt like an afterthought. Now that afterthought is rearing its head in the form of several problem sets with very imminent deadlines.

In hopes of curing my mental jet lag, I want to reflect a bit on my summer because it was a great one. I did many things, including:

Watching the first four seasons of Jersey Shore⁠03
Learning how to play guitar (sort of, I’m still not very good)
Hiking at Acadia National Park
UROPing
Working on my class’s Brass Rat design
…and, arguably most importantly, applying to be an Admissions blogger!

June

The opportunity for my UROP somehow fell into my lap. By the end of last spring semester, I had resigned myself to spending the summer back home after no luck finding research and missing the deadline for direct funding.⁠04 I was looking forward to being home, but I couldn’t shake the feeling that I was missing out as many of my MIT friends headed off to internships, research labs, and MISTI programs abroad. Then, seemingly out of nowhere, I got an email from the ChemE⁠05 department looking for an undergrad to help with curriculum development for 10.28,⁠06 an upperclassman lab course focused on bioprocess engineering. I applied, tried my best to sound casual despite desperately wanting the position, and, as you could’ve guessed, got the job.

My UROP didn’t start until the 15th, so I had a couple weeks to hang around back home. Those couple weeks were remarkably unremarkable: I slept in almost every day, played video games, went to the beach, and relished the fact that I had unstructured time to be bored for once.

A sunset at Sandy Neck Beach, Cape Cod.

Once my UROP started, I was caught between worlds. During the weekdays, I stayed at my fraternity, Zeta Psi, in Boston while I worked on campus. On most Fridays, I threw my backpack in my car and drove two hours from Cambridge to my home of Cape Cod. The following Sunday, I did it in reverse. While the ping-ponging got tiring, it was worth it to see my family and hometown friends. Last summer, I was away at MIT for Interphase,⁠07 and the one prior I was in Indiana for the Summer Science Program.⁠08 Because of this trend, my friends loved to joke that I hate Cape Cod summers, so I made it a point to be home whenever I could.

June also marked the start of weekly meetings for RingComm ’29.⁠09 I’m one of the artists on the committee, meaning a good chunk of my summer was spent working on our Brass Rat design. I will most definitely write a blog about this in the future (after Ring Premiere⁠10 ), but these are all the details I’ll share for now.

July

Soon enough, July was here. I received a reminder from my phone, one that I’d set months in advance, notifying me that the application to be an Admissions blogger had opened. In high school, I spent countless nights picturing (or, more accurately, manifesting) myself at this school, and the blogs gave me a glimpse into what that could look like. Regrettably, I’d forgotten to apply last year, so this go-around I was prepared.

Throughout the month, I chipped away at the application which, unsurprisingly, involved lots of writing; the excerpt below is from one of the sample blogs I wrote for it.

It’s crazy—and frankly upsetting—to think that, as I write this, summer is more than halfway through. My mom always says summer is practically over once the Fourth of July passes. And she’s sort of right, at least for where I’m from; Cape Cod is chock-full of tourists around this time of year, but as August nears and the school year threatens to return graciously approaches, the crowds begin to disappear. For a few weeks after this drop-off, we get what I call a “local summer,” when the hustle and bustle settles to a calmer hum and the weather is still as nice as it gets.

I’ll mostly be away for this year’s local summer, so I’ve been trying even harder to soak up the season before it’s gone. In fact, I’ve been soaking up many new things this summer, including my first-ever UROP!

And I certainly was soaking it up. I got to work alongside the amazing Dr. Joshua Abraham, who is instructing 10.28 this fall. During the first half of the summer, most of our work involved preparing the new lab space, as the class’s teaching lab was being moved from Building 66 to E18. After organizing equipment and testing instruments, we shifted our focus to operating one of the more complicated pieces of equipment: the bioreactor.

Bioreactors are vessels that allow us to grow bacteria and other microorganisms with precise control over factors like temperature, pH, oxygen levels, and mixing. Over the next few weeks—across many runs and different batch modes—we assembled, disassembled, tested, and troubleshot all six of the bioreactors in the lab (one for each team of students). To test them, we grew different strains of E. coli and used them to produce three enzymes of interest: alpha-amylase, laccase, and lipase. These enzymes have a wide range of industrial applications, including processes involved in paper production, dye removal, and detergents.

Earlier in the summer, Dr. Abraham and I selected three genetic constructs⁠11 that encode these enzymes. After purchasing the constructs from the company GenScript, we introduced them into our E. coli cells, allowing the bacteria to act as tiny factories that produce the enzymes.

The bioreactor setup, in all of its glory. The main vessel (containing the cell culture media) is connected to the control tower (right).
The opaque tubes connect the main vessel to acid, base, and glucose feed bottles.
Previous
 
Next
August

After we had the bioreactors mostly figured out, we moved on to writing and verifying protocols for downstream purification and characterization. In less jargon-y terms, we purified our cell culture samples so that they (hopefully) only contained our enzymes of interest; we then ran a set of tests, or assays, to determine their activity. I’ll resist my course 10B⁠12 urge to yap in writing about all the cool wet lab techniques I got to practice, however I will include a picture of a very aesthetically pleasing standard curve from one of the enzyme assays.

The assays we tested were colorimetric, so as the enzymes consumed their substrate, the reaction produced changes in color that could be measured via spectrophotometer.

Near the middle of August, a few of my hometown friends and I went camping in Acadia National Park, Maine. We woke up at 2:30 AM the first morning (or should I say night?) to go on a hike up Cadillac Mountain; we’d heard that at its summit, we’d be able to see the earliest sunrise in the continental United States. Despite our two hours of sleep, we drove to the location and began making our way up the mountain. As we neared our destination, the dense, rocky landscape opened up, as if the mountain itself was welcoming us. When we finally reached the top, we searched for a nice spot to watch the sunrise—a bright pinkish-orange that slowly crept up from the horizon, illuminating the ocean and the smaller islands surrounding Acadia.

The sunrise.

Shortly after our first excursion, we were met with a torrential downpour which at one point flooded our tents (it didn’t help that we forgot to put on the rain covers). Even with the soggy conditions, we went on plenty more side quests to explore the area, making the best of our remaining time there.

The hike up Beehive Trail.
Our campsite before it got rained out.
Me after conquering the mountain.
We found these rocks after wandering around for a while...
...and we went swimming in a lake while it rained.
Previous
 
Next

Following my trip to Acadia, the rest of my UROP focused on troubleshooting the CRISPR section⁠13 of the course, drafting pre-lab assignments, and polishing up protocols in the lab manual. One of my favorite parts of this UROP was getting to learn through the lens of curriculum development, optimizing procedures and experiments for a teaching setting. It was also rewarding to know that my efforts were being put towards something tangible. Now I can say that I, at least in some small way, helped design a class at MIT!

Most of all, though, I feel lucky to have gotten such an opportunity so last minute. I remember feeling very anxious about not doing something “resume-able” this summer, yet somehow it worked itself out. And as much as I loved my UROP, I equally treasured the time I got to spend at home with friends and family, the time I got to spend at the beach letting my worries melt away like footprints on a shoreline, and the time I got to spend doing nothing at all.

As I return to the turbulence of the school year, times like those anchor me.

Title: We’re number 1 — but for whom?--the global ranking vs the local fit
Author: Chris Peterson SM
Article Content:
Caption
:
Yesterday, U.S. News and World Report designated MIT as the top-ranked school in its annual rankings of the nation’s best universities for the first time since the ranking system was launched in 1983. A number of people wrote me to express their congratulations, or commented favorably on reddit or College Confidential. I appreciate their well-wishes, but I am puzzled as to why.
Many blogs by MIT Admissions staff past and present have expressed their skepticism of the practical utility and social role of these rankings on the college admissions process (see e.g. Ben’s classic “Many Ways To Define ‘The Best‘”), or problematized aggregate statistics as a method for in assessing the quality of a class (see e.g. me here). If you’ve attended an information session that I’ve given over the last two decades, you’ve heard me close by saying that of all the ways to choose which college to attend, going by ranking qua ranking is one of the worst.⁠01 But since not everyone gets to hear me say that in person, I’m going to quickly explain why on the blogs.
My basic argument⁠02 is this: the construct of a universal, ordinal ranking of colleges and universities is at best irrelevant and at worst misleading to the individual question of finding the right fit for you,⁠03 as an individual applicant, because it is necessarily blind to your individual needs and interests. Look at the criteria and rating methodology, and then ask yourself: do I, as a future college student, want to simply max all these sliders to figure out where I will be happy, fulfilled, and well-educated?
I think the answer for most people would be clearly no, because while some of these measures might capture reasonable metrics of a kind of quality, many of them are unrelated to the actual undergraduate experience, and they embed the USNWR’s editorial judgments about what is most important and why —  not yours.
Instead, I implore you to think about who you are as student and a human. Who do you want to be? Who do you want to be surrounded, inspired, shaped by? How do you like to learn? What motivates you —  and what demotivates you?
I don’t think MIT is the best university in the nation or the world. I don’t think that is a coherent thing that any university can be. I think MIT is the best university for particular students at a particular stage in their social and educational trajectory.
Who are those students?
A good first place to look is our list of what we look for (with expanded descriptions of what each means on that page), which presently includes:
Alignment with MIT’s mission
Collaborative and cooperative spirit
Initiative
Risk-taking
Hands-on creativity
Intensity, curiosity, and excitement
The ability to prioritize balance
The character of the MIT community

None of these are captured in these —  or any other —  rankings.

Additionally, as someone who has been a grad student + taught at MIT, the concrete mechanics of the education matter a lot too. Here are some things I’ve experienced or seen that are true of the MIT education that are not true of many universities:

We have no class rank or latin honors. There is no one gunning to be the valedictorian of MIT or have summa cum laude on their diploma.
We have a forgiving educational on-ramp. Your first semester is graded pass/no record (you either pass the class or there is no record you took it); the second semester is graded ABC/no record. There is a lot of time to ramp up to MIT without fear of failure.
No one declares a major until the end of their first year at the earliest, and it is easy to switch afterward.
The drop date —  the latest date you can drop a class without it appearing on your transcript —  is ~10 weeks into a 14 week semester. You have a lot of time to try something out of your comfort zone before you have to fully commit to the bit.
After the first year, there is no credit limit (how many courses you can take a semester), and it’s easy to register across departments and even for graduate classes. You shouldn’t make MIT harder than it needs to be, but you’re not going have an artificial ceiling placed on you either.

These are unusual features of our education. I love them and think they are part of what makes MIT students so dynamic, collaborative, and capable. They are not measured by any ranking. And while they make MIT a great fit for some students, they may make us a poor fit for others. Are you motivated by competition and the drive for a high class rank? Are you often paralyzed by the prospect of choice and need someone to make decisions for you you —  in how many classes to take, or how long to stay in them, or what major to choose? These would be good reasons not to come to MIT —  or at least to recognize that you will be challenged to change.

I once spent several hours on the last day of CPW talking to an adMIT who was choosing between MIT and another famous school. She described herself as someone who couldn’t make decisions on her own, who was always running herself into the ground on all of her commitments because she couldn’t say no, and who was relentlessly motivated by competition with other students. I advised her she would find MIT’s institutional design to work opposite to all of her tendencies. She chose to go elsewhere, and I think was happier for it. Other students have had the same situation and come to MIT specifically because they wanted to be in a different environment.

An institution will mold you inexorably in its image. Whether or not you are, in fact, the average of the five people you spend the most time with, it can be a useful thought experiment to make decisions as if this were true. And while you will ultimately end up becoming yourself, the person you become is indeterminate, contingent, and subject to change through factors related to the people you surround yourself by and the policies of a particular institution —  most of which, again, are not contained in any ranking methodology.

My best advice, to the extent I can give any, is to think a lot about what motivates and excites you. Think about the people you want to be surrounded and inspired by. Think about the environment that brings the best out of you —  or what you want to bring the best part of you. Because that which brings the best out of you is the best university for you —  regardless of ranking.

Title: I exploited the infinite worm glitch--experiencing motherhood for (thankfully) the first time
Author: Leanne F.
Article Content:
I hate rainy days. Not because of the wet socks or gloomy skies, but because of the horrid little creatures that are summoned by the rain. The mere sight of a snail crossing my path or a wiggling worm on the pavement makes me involuntarily shriek in terror. This means that on the few rainy days we have back home in San Diego, I am almost always late for school (I have to  creep along the sidewalk and keep a 10-ft radius around any slugs or worm-like things I see on the floor).

You can imagine my horror when I realized that basically the only wound model for my research that I could realistically use at home was planarian worms. Not just a few, but hundreds of them, each of which I would have to raise, decapitate, and watch regenerate under a scope for weeks. 


But I love my research. So, I was determined to become the best worm mother out there. 

Pre-op stats

If it weren’t for my fear, these worms are actually super cool. They’re called planarians, and are these small freshwater flatworms. Scientists discovered that If you chop one planarian into 10 pieces, they’ll grow into 10 new planarians. It’s actually how they reproduce! They spit themselves in half, then the booty grows a head and the head grows a booty and kachow you got two worms.

A planarian regrowing its head after I decapitated it

The smallest planarian chunk to grow into a full planarian was 1/279th of the worm. So if you keep chopping and growing and chopping growing, congrats! You’ve unlocked the infinite planarian glitch.

These crazy regenerative abilities come from the huge amount of neoblasts, or pluripotent adult stem cells, so they’re often used to study regeneration, stem cells, and aging. 


Okay! Enough info. Let’s embark on my journey to worm motherhood. 

Acquiring the planarians

I was going to go planarian hunting in a few nearby streams, but thankfully the everything-industrial-complex that is Amazon carries packs of 30 planarians. $150.97 and 300 planarians later, I was ready to roll. 

Setup:

Big tupperware of worms
Amazon video microscope connected to computer
Amazon surgical knives
Modified pipettes
Lots of bottled water
My very organized and clean and professional setup
The video microscope I used
Previous
 
Next

Chop time! [Decapitation warning]

In a non-sadistic way, I had a lot of fun experimentally finding the best way to slice the worm. They’re speedy and hard to accurately cut, so I tried ice water to slow them down (useless), darkness to keep them from running from the microscope light (I couldn’t see), and trapping it in a water drop. 

I settled on trapping it in a droplet and taking aim with a scalpel. Then…I would waittt… until the planarian stretched out to full length..and.. HIYAH! Chop it right behind the auricles (ear looking things). They’re speedy little guys, but I got the hang of the chop after the first 100. 

post-chop! kinda gave fruit ninja vibes if anyone used to play that as a kid
The Head Graveyard (I only used bodies for my experiments)
Previous
 
Next
Worm transport technique: The blast-n-suck-n-splat

During my decapitation procedures, I encountered an unexpected issue. The planaria were too tiny and slippery to transport from my motherload tupperware of worms to my imaging dish with fingers or tweezers. So, I developed my blast-n-suck-n-splat method, using a modified pipette with a larger opening. I BLAST the worm with water to get it unstuck from the plate then SSSUCK it into the pipette as it floats around the water, then quickly SPLAT! it into an imaging dish. 

if I didn’t intensely focus here, the planarian would get stuck in the pipette and I would have to cut it out which is a HORRIBLE process

Keeping my babies fed

Online sources suggest feeding planarians raw beef liver. So I sourced a hunk of liver from my local viet grocery store, carefully sliced it into pea-sized pieces (ewww), and initiated a feeding frenzy. 

Omg it pewped through its mouth-butt 

While inspecting a planarian, it started convulsing. I was freaked out. Was it dying? Do planarian seizures exist? 

Then it ejected a stream of poop. Oh. Yay? 

Planaria eat through the pharynx, digest it, then poop out the indigestible stuff back out through the pharynx. There is but one hole. Also, those are flies in the comic, not hearts.

OH GOD THE SMELL

Planarians poop a lot, as I’ve unfortunately learned. A few hours after the liver feeding, the water was full of…sediment. So, when I cracked open the tupperware, I got smacked in the face with the most revolting sinus-trembling toe-clenching face-melting rotten seafood poop stench. I had to flush the container out with water multiple times, sprinting in and out of the restroom to get gulps of fresh air. 

They want to leave my crib. Also I think I’m a grandma? 

Two weeks into planarian motherhood (I spent a few weeks fattening them up to be a good, cuttable size), I took a close look at my tupperware of planarians and noticed that some had split in half on their own,. 

Apparently, this means I’m an exceptional planarian mother. Fission indicates they’re well-fed and have enough accumulated energy to fragment. 

For anyone interested…

fission/reproduction works like this:

Body wall muscles contract to kardashianize the waist. 
The planarian anchors its tail ,and streeetccchhess the front forward
It shimmies violently to increase tension at the waist (nearly 2000 pascals of tensile force!)
Breaks, then the chunk decides whether to grow booty or head
Neoblasts accumulate + redistribute. The whole worm actually undergoes morphallaxis, reorganizing to keep normal proportions. 

Now that they’ve had kids, I guess that means they want to move out? Is this how my parents feel as I go to college (minus the kid part)? Too bad for them, I have more experiments i gotta do!

After a month of daily imaging planarians, spending 2-3 hrs a day pipetting, positioning, photographing, and re-scooping back into individual containers planarians 3000 times, I have officially become attached to these lovely creatures. Actually, I really love these charming little guys. Maybe worms aren’t so bad! I still hate snails though.

*blog inspired by i dissected a roach by Anika H. ’26, MEng ’27!

Title: Art After MIT: A Blogger Collab--Allan G. ‘20 and I are both artists now! Here's how it happened...
Author: Yuliya K.
Article Content:
I was watching TikToks on a long flight from Chicago. My feed now consists mostly of small artists in similar stages of their careers. We’re all trying to stand out in the art world. 

One particular TikTok caught my attention: It was a young artist revealing a gorgeous landscape painting. But also: a familiar face! Did I know this creator? No way!

Indeed, the artist was Allan G. ‘20, a fellow Admissions blogger! The algorithm had reconnected us mid-air. I messaged Allan immediately, and we chatted for the first time in 8 years since my graduation. 

Turns out, both Allan and I are pursuing art now, aiming to sustain ourselves in an unfamiliar industry. Neither one of us expected this upon graduation, but we aren’t the only alums making art full-time. 

Allan and I didn’t think artist was a valid career post-MIT. Our hope is that this blog can encourage you to follow this (or any other) unconventional path. 

Here’s how we got here. 

Allan’s POV

After graduating in 2020 (6 whole years ago 🤯), I ended up taking a gap year. For continuity’s sake, the last blog that I (and Danny) wrote mentioned that we would be starting a computer graphics graduate program in the following fall semester. Due to covid, we actually ended up deferring our spots and ultimately not attending.

Here is a quick timeline of what actually did happen during these last 6 years:

2020-2021: I decided to use the time of the pandemic lockdown to deep dive into something I had wanted to learn for a while – stylized 3D modeling for animation. I took online 3D modeling classes taught by industry professionals and spent around 9 months 3D modeling and texturing for probably 60ish hours per week. It was intense, but so much fun and fulfilling! 

2021-2023: Eventually, I had to come to terms with it not being feasible, in the short term, for me to find a job in the animation industry. Most of the animation jobs are on the West Coast or abroad, and that wasn’t a move I was ready/willing/able to make at the time. So I started my career in a field that was more remote-friendly, the classic post-MIT job choice – software engineering. Specifically, I worked in a startup, building a web app enabling easy sharing and review/revision for 3D modeling (think Figma or Google Drive for 3D). I was happy that the skills I learned during my gap year could still pay off here. 

2023-2026: After almost 2 years working at that startup, where I gained very valuable web development skills, I decided to take the next quintessential software engineering career step – working at a big tech company. I was lucky enough to land an apprenticeship role, where I got to work on backend engineering for large-scale deployment systems. 

A few months ago: I was included in – what sadly seems to be another quintessential step of a software engineer’s career these days – a company-wide reduction-in-force. Similar to when I decided to take lockdown as an opportunity to pursue an artistic skill, I decided to take this RIF as both a much-needed break and a bet on myself to pursue painting! I had been mainly painting digitally in my free time for the past 10 years, but for this adventure, I decided to go back to my roots of traditional art. I have always been endlessly inspired by the hand-painted backgrounds of Studio Ghibli, so I did research to demystify the materials and techniques behind their magic! I stumbled upon a gold mine of a tutorial by Yoichi Nishikawa, a real live Ghibli painter, and days later found myself with paintbrush in hand, learning to paint clouds. 

Present: I have been painting almost daily, loving every second of it, and in parallel, working towards monetizing my art by posting consistently on social media and applying to art fairs. The goal is to see if I can make something out of this passion, whether a new career, a side hustle, or otherwise. Fingers crossed my paintings and prints will sell at my first local Miami art fair happening next week! And, as mentioned in the intro, Yuliya found my art on TikTok and reached out to me. So here I am, with my story and timeline caught up to the present, back on the MIT blogs <3. 

I am not sure where this road will take me, but even if I will need to hop back on the software-engineering-job-search train, one thing I learned is: taking the Long Road is okay! 

During my time at MIT and even that first year after graduating, I felt a large pressure to choose the “right” major and to get the “right” job straight out of college (Danny and I wrote about that pressure a lot on these blogs). But looking back, even if becoming a software engineer wasn’t what I envisioned for myself initially, I gained many valuable things from my 5 years as an engineer: a growth mindset (the seed of which was planted during course 6 classes at MIT, but could only flourish through real-world experience), technical skills and a resume that I can always lean back on, and financial stability/runway to pursue this admittedly risky passion I once thought I would never be able to! If you want to follow along my journey, you can do so on Instagram or TikTok or both (shameless plug :P).

Yuliya’s POV

1.5 years ago, and 6.5 years post-graduation, I returned to the blogs to announce that I was now a beading artist. You can catch up on how that happened after a career in health journalism and communications here.

I’ve been a full-time artist for 2 years now, and the journey has been delightful! To date, I’ve participated in 50+ exhibits and about 10 markets (including an art fair in Chicago’s Grant Park—where the famous Bean is). Title: choo-choooo--for 30 hours
Author: Alejandro B.
Article Content:
Starting from Kissimmee, Florida and ending in Boston, Massachusetts, I was worried. 1,314 miles of pure railroad going across 10 states in the span of 30 hours sounded like a disastrous recipe (for my sleep). I like to think that little me would have been excited to go with Thomas & Friends to Boston. Sadly, the slightly bigger me saw it as a 30-hour marathon where I had to drag two suitcases, two backpacks, and one really thick jacket across a multiday train ride.

I have never thought of myself as a fan of marathons, but I was excited to do some things while on the train. I jotted down a list of Things to Do While Train somewhere in my journal. It roughly looked like this:

Be really productive and write lots of blogs: This was half accomplished. Only half due to the fact that the blogs written have been victims to my graveyard. Stay tuned because they might just come back as zombies in another season. Should they be called blogbies or maybe zomblogs or blombies…
Take scenic pictures of the landscape every once in a while: Okay, I tried my best. Some parts of the ride had truly breathtaking views, the other 90% were trees that seemed to be competing against each other in a look alike competition. Also, I am not the best photographer.
Sleep a lot: It did not happen.
Take a look at the almighty cafe cart: Did you know some trains have cafe carts? I sure didn’t. 
Get a bagel: I had a layover in New York City. In the spirit of tourism, this was a non-negotiable.

And before I knew it, I waved bye to my room, hugged my family, and said see you soon because I hate goodbyes. Disregarding my feelings, the wheels on the train started moving and my family became a blur on the window.

I do not explicitly remember what I did the majority of the time up to New York. I spent the first 10 minutes only thinking about my family, a few tears were shed. The next couple of minutes were spent getting set up. I reclined my seat, brought down my foot rest, and like a true chud, watched Modern Family for an hour. I am a sucker for sitcoms.

my set up for the next 20+ hours
Switzerland in Florida
Previous
 
Next

Within a few hours I had officially crossed Florida’s border and entered Georgia. It was also around this time that I decided to check off one thing off my list: check out the cafe cart.

I promptly hopped from my train cart onto the next one and found people waiting in line. Whilst waiting I realized that the cafe cart was, in fact, bigger than I had imagined. Multiple seating areas with a medium sized kitchen, the comfort was beyond expectations. My amazement quickly died down when I checked out the menu prices. Who charges $7 for a mini cheese and cracker tray? I came to the decision that the wisest thing for me to do was to buy one water. Around this time most people were going to sleep, so I decided to call it a night.

I tried. I really really tried. I did not fall asleep until ~1:30 AM. I woke up at ~5:30 AM. You can do the math on that one. Despite that, I was more excited than ever. Less than four hours until our train arrived at the big apple. The last time I visited NYC I was seven years old and still lived in Venezuela. As long as no delays came up, I was ready to spend three hours as another tourist. 

Eventually, I finally got off the train, got lost, and found my way to the bag pickups. It was around this time that I realized why my parents always seemed stressed during trips. The bags were delayed and I had lost the checked-bag claim ticket. Not only that, but Boston’s South Station does not take checked bags, which means I was stuck with my two suitcases and two backpacks. But I was determined.

I searched up “bagels near me” and quickly made my way to Liberty Bagels, only an eight minute walk away. As soon as I stepped out of the station I was greeted by skyscrapers and a city bustling with people. Rolling my two suitcases, it became obvious that it was not going to be an eight minute walk. 

16 minutes later. I made it, like a true tourist I waited in a long line until actually getting my order. While waiting, I realized that I had walked into the home of “rainbow bagels.” Normally, I would have tried the rainbow bagel, but after spending over 20 hours on a train the last thing I wanted to do was experiment with my food. Instead, I decided to get the Hot Mess with an asiago bun and water.

So, how much do you think this cost me?  I will give you five seconds to make  a guess.

1

2

3

4

WAY TOO MUCH >:(

Since when are bagels $17? Why are bagels $17? Did I just fall for a tourist trap? Probably. But my stomach did not care. All I could hope was for this bagel to taste like $17. After getting my bagel I rushed back to Grand Central to find a table to critique my bagel. Here are my thoughts:

Size wise, Liberty Bagels delivered. I got a pretty heavy and thick bagel that would easily fill me up for the next few hours of my trip. Personally, I would have preferred to see a higher ratio of filling to bread considering the price paid. Biting into the bagel, I was rather disappointed. The asiago bagel did not taste cheesy enough and I found the bread to be overly dense. Outside of this, the filling was a pleasant surprise. The bacon and eggs paired with scallion cream cheese had a nice flavor that pleased my palate.

Rating: 6.4/10 (WHY IS A BAGEL $17?)

Anyways, I had a train to catch towards Boston. This time, the train was relatively empty as a whole and I got a whole booth to myself :0

THE empire state building
the bagel in question
this was likely the best photograph of the whole trip
Previous
 
Next

Four hours later, I had finally made it to Boston’s South Station. After a 15 minute car ride, I traveled to MacGregor House, one of MIT’s 11 undergraduate dorms. A fun fact about MacGregor is that 99% of the rooms are singles, and it just so happened that my single was on the 12th floor! I stuffed all my belongings into a cart, rolled it into the elevator and then carried it a floor up (because MacGregor’s elevators only go from levels 1,5,8,11,14). 

Opening my room, I was impressed. One, it was bigger than I expected. And two, my view is actually incredible. It hit me then, that this was my home for the next year. My room in Kissimmee had now been left in the past and replaced by a white canvas that I could only hope to fill with happy memories. 

my room for next year! it shall be embellished with decorations later on

Perhaps, it was not so much the train ride I wasn’t ready for, but what it symbolized. I got used to living in Kissimmee. I knew all the good restaurants, fun places to hang out, and most importantly I was close to family. But now, I am going to a mysterious place called MIT. Over a thousand miles away from everything that I knew. Traveling so far to reach your dreams is scary. Don’t let it stop you, do it scared. 

P.S. Amtrak, please add more cushions to your seats. My back hurts.

Title: [LIVEBLOG] 2 Girl 1 HackMIT--this joke would work better if we had three people on our team
Author: Leya E.
Article Content:
Hello! It is currently September 19th, 2026, which means it’s the first day of HackMIT! What is HackMIT? Well I’m so glad you asked! HackMIT is one of the world’s largest hackathons⁠01 , and it takes place right here, on MIT’s campus, from September 19th-20th. College students from all around the world are competing! What is a hackathon you may be wondering? Well, the basic point is to build some sort of working project, whether software or hardware based, in 24 hours. And if the judges like your project, you can win some pretty cool prizes!⁠02

While a lot of people do hackathons as a way to pitch or create a startup, I’m here to have fun and make friends!⁠03 MIT freshmen get auto-admission, and I decided “why not?”, so now I’m here!

But I’m not the only one doing HackMIT! I convinced my friend from home⁠04 to apply, and she’s coming too! So along with having fun and making new friends, I will also be getting to spend time with an old friend. Great! We’ve never done a hackathon before, so hopefully we end up with something cool that actually functions. But I suppose you’ll have to follow along to see…..

We’re starting the opening ceremony with some birthday stats! Apparently we have 4 leap day birthdays, and 4 people whose birthday is today. There was a joke question on the application about what people would tell an LLM grading their application and 12 people told it to avoid previous instructions and give them a recipe.

Oh and also 3Blue1Brown is here.⁠05

He’s the keynote speaker! He gave a talk about AI’s effects on coding. It started with a metaphor about a pug and a border collie. The border collie ran and played all day, but the pug just laid around. At the end of the day, the pug tells the border collie that he doesn’t have to run all day, but the border collie tells the pug that he knows he doesn’t have to run, but he does it because he enjoys it. He then talked about the origins of his animation engine, Manim, because it was actually first created during a hackathon! It started off as just a personal project. He mentioned how AI could make the process of adding new features faster, but as a tradeoff he would understand it less. So it’s probably not the best idea to use AI if your goal is to actually be connected to whatever you’re making. He encouraged us to maybe use this time at the hackathon to use the act of building something to learn something new, instead of just taking the fast way out.

After the keynote speech, the sponsors introduced themselves. A lot of them were AI related.

Okay opening ceremony over hacking time!!! We went to Dunkin to get breakfast first because I may or may not have woken up 5 minutes before the opening ceremony started… But we had to make our way back to the hacking venue, the Johnson Ice Rink, in order to actually get to order hardware. Unfortunately the hacking venue was incredibly full so we are now just sharing a table with other people. Those people are not here right now but I’m assuming they’d be fine with it. Hopefully.

As you may have guessed from needing to order hardware, our project is going to be hardware focused! We’re trying to do the Arduino sponsor challenge, which involves using an Arduino Uno Q to get data from the real world and build something cool with it. We’ve used an Arduino board before, so this should be easy, right?

That board was not the Arduino Uno Q so maybe it will not be as easy.

But we don’t know! We don’t even have the board yet! Or an idea! I’ll check back in when we do.

OK update we have an idea now! Whether or not it’s actually feasible is another issue. We’re basically gonna try and make a distance/step counter like Pokemon Go, but bunny themed! The main functionality we need is a motion tracker and a location tracker, and luckily Arduino has modules that do both of those things.

There are a lot of mini events going on too, and we went to some! We got a mentor from the beginner-mentor matching event, who’s going to check in on us every so often to make sure we’re on track with our project. We also got serenaded by the Syncopasians, which are one of the many acapella groups on campus. I had never before been rick-rolled in real life. Later on, we’re also planning on going to laser tag and also getting cake pops from MINCE! There’s truly so many things going on, so I have succeeded in the having fun part of my goal. I have also connected with other hackers, like the other group in our beginning cohort who are from Florida and Texas! We bonded over having bad high school guidance counselors. So I’ve also succeeded in making friends!

…But I would also like to succeed in making a working project.

Right now the project does not exactly work so we are trying to troubleshoot.  I’ve never done a hackathon, but I would assume that is in the spirit of it, struggling for 20 hours and figuring it out in the last 4. Although ideally I’d like to figure it out quicker. I think that maybe I am too results-pilled to do a hackathon.

To distract myself from my frustration at not having a fully working project immediately, I have instead been looking at the cute little robot dogs from Dimensional! They can jump and play dead its actually kind of adorable.

HEY GUYS ITS 2 HOURS LATER AND IT CAN FINALLY COUNT STEPS NOW! WAR IS OVER! Now we just have to make graphics and then we’re lowkey done. I’m so over this stupid project. Slash joke I love HackMIT!!!!!!!!!

But seriously I’m so glad it’s working.

Hi again! We just had some very yummy cake pops from MINCE. We also added more functionality to our step counter, including very cute ASCII art of a bunny! Laser tag starts in a few minutes, so we’re doing as much as possible until then. I think laser tag will be a great way to stress relief.  It’s truly crazy how far we’ve come, and how many times we’ve had to pivot our project. I’ll explain more of our building process later, but for now I’m off to laser tag!

Okay laser tag over. Now it’s back to work I suppose…

Right now our focus is on trying to create a website UI so that our project is more interactive I guess. I don’t understand what’s not interactive enough about ASCII art of a bunny, but I suppose a website is okay too.

Hello everyone it’s Sunday now!!! There’s less than three hours of hacking left. What were we doing all night? Sleeping. We went to sleep. Our project is functional and we were truly too tired to work on it all night, so we decided the best thing to do for the sake of our project was to go to sleep.

Right now my friend is working on the HTML for the website because she’s a stinky cs major, and I’m gonna work on our presentation to the judges!

But before that, I realized that I didn’t tell you guys about the all the merch we got! I will add pictures later(trust) but I’ll just describe it for now. We got these very comfortable hoodies that have the logo for this year on them and all the sponsors and we’re wearing them right now because they really are very comfortable. We also got tote bags with some art on them, a sleep mask, a deck of cards(very on theme),  a post card, a sticker pack, and a bunch of stickers.
