But the best thing is definitely the cute little yellow bunny plushie we got. I love HackMIT. The art direction is literally so awesome this year.

 

IT’S OVER! Hacking is officially over and judging starts in about an hour! And also our project actually works!!! This is awesome. Okay I will be back with a detailed description of project later now I’m gonna take my friend on a tour of campus!!!

OKAY JUDGING IS OVER!!! I THINK WE’RE FREE! At least until the closing ceremony. I’m waiting for some sort of message that we are actually free because there are simply too many people in this ice rink.

In the meantime, here’s the link to our project on github :3 https://github.com/beao35/steptracker-hackmit2026

our cutesy webpage since i imagine most readers do not have access to an arduino uno q

It uses some built-in functionality from the Arduino App Lab to detect up-down motion and create a local web page that will get an inputted step goal and display a person’s current steps, along with a cute picture of a bunny. The only thing we were not able to do with the webpage is make the font comic sans.

We were originally much more ambitious with the scope of our project. We wanted to create some sort of combination step counter and task manager that would encourage college students to get exercise by walking to get to their classes/events! But a large delay in obtaining the hardware, as well as in understanding the hardware, led us to narrow our scope a little. We used the movement module to detect up-down movement, but went through random period where the code simply would not compile for seemingly no reason. We even had to resort to asking an LLM, which did not help us. Eventually we were able to get it to work in part due to superstition, like waiting until the CPU usage on the board was below 6-7%…

We also had to relearn how to use HTML as we were both very rusty. And getting Python to talk to JavaScript is also kind of complicated! But a good thing about the Arduino App Lab(and most other apps that you would use to program) is that it has documentation that explains what a lot of functions do! So a lot of reading was done.

It’s honestly a pretty simple project compared to how much suffering it caused us… But I think it’s also pretty cool! It’s awesome to see how you can combine C, Python, HTML, JavaScript, and CSS to make something that actually like works. And is even vaguely functional! If not completely obsolete due to the existence of phones. And even throughout all the struggle, and there was a lot of it, I think I still had a lot of fun! I actually get why people like Hackathons now. Making something functional in 24 hours is a lot harder than you think it is, but the relief you feel when it actually works is like the best feeling in the world. And HackMIT is lowkey a great environment to feel that feeling, because there were so many fun things going on that even throughout the struggle, it never felt too bad.

And yes, our project is pretty simple compared to what some other teams created, but in times like these I think of the wisdom I learned from cross country in high school. It doesn’t matter if you’re not as impressive as everyone else, because at least you’re in the room! Some incredibly successful startup is probably being pitched right now, and I can say I was in the room where it happened!! That’s pretty cool. So no matter what the results of the judging are, I think my HackMIT experience was a success.

See you at closing ceremony!

Um so I did not actually end up going to closing ceremony because it started late. But I’m assuming it was very cool! Thank you for reading my HackMIT experience, and a big shoutout to the HackMIT team for creating that experience! If you’re a high schooler who wants to do a hackathon at MIT, the HackMIT team also puts on Blueprint in the Spring, so look out for that.

Title: liquid nitrogen and nothing else--🧄
Author: Joy X.
Article Content:
About a year ago, Ellie posted a blog about what I thought would be my (first and) last year of Mathcamp⁠01 . In hindsight, it’s no surprise that I applied to return as a JC a few months later. 

And when my offer popped up in my inbox, I thought perhaps the universe had the same sense of humor as me, because suddenly an idea for the greatest parody blog just popped into existence.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Like my ancestors before me, this year at Mathcamp, I was a LN2JC–a title I particularly like, because it looks like a 2-factor authentication code. The LN2 stands for Liquid Nitrogen gas (N^2), with which we made liquid nitrogen ice cream. Making liquid nitrogen ice cream is a long standing Mathcamp tradition that happens every week during Academic Advisor meetings. 

The JC stands for… JC. I made the mistake of thinking it stands for “Junior Counselor” once before, but it turns out that JC doesn’t actually stand for anything. Perhaps this year it stands for Juggling Clown, or Jolly Capper. I won’t elaborate in this blog, because as the title suggests, I can’t write about anything other than liquid nitrogen. 

~~~~~~Week -5~~~~~~~

In June, I learned how to get quotes from liquid nitrogen companies, and read up on liquid nitrogen safety. After realizing that sometimes you needed to call companies (scary! I was actually petrified of talking to real people on the phone before becoming a JC) when they ghost your emails, my co-LN2JC, Keti, and I settled on a welding place that sold liquid nitrogen. They had the best (worst?) address imaginable: 67 Chad Ln. 

~~~~~~Week 0~~~~~~~

We passed through the trials of obtaining liquid nitrogen in the first place (we brought the dewar–the insulated container–in a car and hugged it on the way there and back) and learning to pronounce dewar (apparently it is not de-war, but dew-ar). Liquid nitrogen is extremely cool; both literally and in the other sense. 

Woahhh mist…

The first flavor we made was perhaps the most classic ice cream flavor of them all: cement.

…just kidding, we were trying to make chocolate ice cream, but we accidentally put wet cement into it. Just kidding (again). We wanted to make Blue Chocolate for whatever reason, but forgot that blue and brown make grey apparently. The chocolate flavor was Keti’s idea, and the cement coloring was mine. You’ll see this theme pop up many times throughout this blog!

I unfortunately don’t have a picture of this, but I think if I insert a picture of wet cement it will be indistinguishable. Rating: 4/5

The other flavors were not as cursed–we had Canada Flavor (maple syrup), Purple Flavor (frozen berries + orange extract—this was the flavor that most people liked the best; it turned out that berries and orange is a pretty good food combination!), and Piña Colada (the vegan flavor, which we turned green with food coloring). I unfortunately don’t have a picture of the Canada Flavor (or should I say FlavoUr), but Ellie made the same flavor exactly one year ago, so I’ll let you go look at that :)

Piña Colada! Rating: 4/5
Purple berry :) Rating: 5/5
Allison (JC)'s dress contrasts very brightly with the neon green ice cream.
Previous
 
Next

 

~~~~~Week 1~~~~~

For the end-of-first-week LN2, we had a theme—Cookie and Carrot Fairy! At Mathcamp, we have a tradition where during every day during TAU–which stands for Time, Academic, Unscheduled, a dedicated time for campers to work on homework for their classes and ask instructors–two JCs go around asking campers if they want cookies or carrots (or neither) to snack on while they work on math. We have a lot of fun with this! Every day is a different theme—the three times I did it so far, we’ve been jesters, video game characters (I had made a Hollow Knight hat and a Among Us hat for this occasion, specifically), and Fireboy and Watergirl from the hit 2009 flash game Fireboy and Watergirl. 

It’s one of the more recognizable traditions at Mathcamp, and so we decided to base our liquid nitrogen ice cream flavors around it. Our first flavor was Fairyland, our vegan flavor with an oat milk base, dragonfruit, strawberry, and mango. It was basically a breakfast fruit mix, but cold–which I liked, because it was essentially the first meal of the day for me (we typically do liquid nitrogen during Academic Advisor meetings, which are 10am-12pm this year. My sleep schedule was not a big fan of this :().

So vibrantly pink! I’m not sure if it was due to food coloring or the natural color of the dragonfruit. In any case, it tasted amazing. Rating: 5/5

The next flavor was Fairy, where we threw together heavy cream, sour candy, twizzlers, jello, and marshmallows. It was an okay flavor; in my opinion, the twizzlers were too crunchy when frozen. 

No live fairies were harmed in the making of this flavor. Rating: 5/5

The third flavor was Cookie fairy, which was a bunch of crushed oreos mixed with mini marshmallows and chocolate syrup. It was a classic cookie and creme flavor. 

Cookie! Rating: 3.5/5

Then was Grass, which, despite my propensity for eating grass (see Cooked Cooking) was not actually grass, but rather Mint Chocolate. I could not in my good conscience feed grass from the ground to campers (maybe grass from the store though…). 

Yum, grass >:) Rating: 4/5
We added in some dirt! (i.e. chocolate syrup). Rating: 4/5
Previous
 
Next

The last flavor was the flavor that I was most excited for–carrot (or maybe more accurately, carrot cake–we also added in cinnamon)! We spent the two hours before our ice cream preparing ingredients, which included grating an entire bag of carrots. It was a controversial flavor. This was our fifth flavor, and we usually do four flavors, and so many people were already tired of ice cream. It was also right before lunch, so maybe not the healthiest time for ice cream. However, one of our Mentors told me that it was her favorite flavor :)

So orange… Rating: 4/5

~~~Week 1.5~~~~~~~

Between week 1 and week 2, we still had a significant amount of liquid nitrogen remaining, so we (well, mostly me–Keti was not very excited about spicy ice cream or pickled ice cream) decided to run a Cursed LN2 Ice Cream event.

The sign for our event! I was really excited about “bees” as a flavor and was searching all over the internet for those fried bees that you sometimes see people selling on the street in certain places. But alas, I could not find any available in Burlington, Vermont (where Mathcamp was located this year).

Two days before the event, I went to the Hannaford’s with not much of a plan except to pick up things that sounded horrible as ice creams. These included things like pickles, goldfish (which was apparently a decent flavor in a past Mathcamp year, so I guess I don’t only have terrible ideas in my head), and mayonnaise. Then, on Tuesday evening, we lugged the 20L dewar of liquid nitrogen down the hill, and commenced the fun. The flavors were as follows:

One: Chocolate Chip. This flavor was by far the least cursed. “But wait!” you say. “Chocolate Chip is a normal flavor of ice cream!” and that is partially true. It was not cursed by taste, but rather cursed because the name held true: it had a normal whipped cream base, but only one chocolate chip in it. We had bought a bag of chocolate chips for use in a previous LN2 session, but it had completely melted from being in the sun for two hours. We refroze the bag, but the chocolate chips had by then merged into one singular big chocolate chip. 

A singular chocolate chip...
That spoon would, in the next second after this photo was taken, be reduced to splinters. Rating: 4/5
Previous
 
Next

Two: Sesame. 

A very delicious sesame flavor. Rating: 3/5

“But wait,” you say again. “That’s still a normal flavor!” and that would be true, except for the fact that I lied. This was not in fact sesame, but rather black pepper. 

Three: Pickles. Keti captured this amazing photo of me pouring pickles into unsuspecting ice cream. 

Wow, I look so happy! Not shown in this photo is me laughing like a maniac the entire two hours of ice cream making. Keti said that it was the happiest I had seemed the entire camp.
Mmmm, mint ice cream… Rating: 5/5
Previous
 
Next

Surprisingly, the pickles ice cream was pretty good, according to most of the people who tried it. We had forgotten to add sugar, which was actually a pretty good outcome—it brought out the tangy flavor of the pickle juice. 

Four: Ketchup. Not many comments here. It just tasted like cold ketchup. I would say that the ketchup made for an especially creamy ice cream, that would inspire a later (non-cursed) ice cream flavor >:) However, according to Keti, this ice cream was especially “eerie” and felt like “eating ketchup with a smooth yogurt consistency” (I’d argue ketchup already has a yogurt-like consistency? but who am I to say…)

Before mixing… it looks like we murdered someone, oops.
After mixing: still looks like we murdered someone. (Nothing was murdered in the process of making this ice cream–except people’s appetites). Rating: 3/5
Previous
 
Next

Five: Buffalo hot sauce. 

It even looks spicy…
Rating: 3/5

So my spice tolerance is super low, and I hate spicy stuff, but this flavor was actually not bad. I only put in around half of the bottle at first, but could barely taste the spice, so I ended up dumping the entire bottle in. I also put in some crushed hot cheetos, which were left over from a previous event that some campers ran: Cursed Oreos (see, I’m not the only one who likes cursed food >:)). They had hot cheeto, wasabi, hot honey, and garlic flavor!

The wasabi looks temptingly like mint…

Garlic was actually a big part of Mathcamp this year. At the beginning of camp, we bought a lot of garlic for some reason, and so some campers decided to devise a way to use it up. Naturally, the method of using up garlic was a garlic eating competition. In the next four weeks, garlic became a big enough thing that campers made garlic butter, garlic and banana pizza, and played garlic chess ⁠02 . 

Ironically, this meant we had to buy more garlic many times. We were also planning to make garlic ice cream, but unfortunately it never happened. However, I actually had garlic ice cream two weeks prior to Mathcamp, in Gilroy, California, the garlic capital of the world. 

My thoughts on Garlic Ice cream: bad at first, but after a while the garlic flavor fades into an aftertaste and it gets better.

Six: Cool Beans. So you’ve most likely realized that I haven’t had complaints about my previous cursed creations, but I will say that this one was genuinely bad, which should concern you. 

It was bad partly because it was extremely salty. I had, because of course I am allergic to ideas that would make for good ice cream, bought canned baked beans instead of something normal, say, red beans. It was also bad because we didn’t clean the bowl between flavors, and so this flavor had not only salty beans, but also chunks of pickles, traces of black pepper, a spicy overtone, and an aftertaste of ketchup.

Oh, and to make things worse, we poured too much liquid nitrogen in it, so it was also rock hard. I had eaten a full small paper cup of all the flavors, but this one was so bad that I could not choke down even half a cup. 

We called it cool beans, and I was inspired by one of the other JCs, Bo, who had told us about a catchphrase that he invented, “beans” (not even “cool beans”. no, something cool happens and he’d just be like. “beans”). While writing this blog, I asked Bo if he’d tried the bean ice cream to get his thoughts on it, and he reported that I had handed him a cup and he had looked concerningly at it. Which, to be fair, is a very reasonable reaction, especially if the ice cream looks like this:

Before freezing… looks like wet concrete.
After freezing… looks like dry concrete. It looks so bad! Perhaps the other flavors could masquerade for better flavors, but there’s no way anyone is mistaking this for anything good. Rating: 0/5
Previous
 
Next

 

we are wizards. maybe evil ones. maybe I’m Voldemort, if he had a nose.
The lighting is really good on this photo! The bowl truly looks like a witch’s cauldron.
Previous
 
Next

~~~~~Week 2~~~~~

Our flavors this week were:

For our vegan flavor, a sprite slushie, mixed with some grenadine syrup (Keti’s idea! You can probably guess, because it was a good idea.). The syrup was a good choice–it lent the sprite a very sweet flavor.

I was secretly hoping that the slushie was going to be slightly fizzy still, but it wasn’t. Rating: 4/5

The second flavor was the one I was most excited for. If you have read this blog up to here, you will realize that this is a bad sign. The flavor was honey crunch, which sounds normal…except for the base:

Mayonnaise.

Mayonnaise! I got this idea because of the ketchup flavor during the Cursed LN2 event–the ketchup had a really nice texture, so I was thinking of other condiments that I make ice cream with. I had heard about mayonnaise being used in baking (mayonnaise cakes are apparently a thing, since mayonnaise is just eggs and oil), so I decided to see if I could pull off a mayonnaise ice cream. 

When I first poured in the mayonnaise and tasted it, I immediately regretted my decisions. Then I poured in condensed milk, sugar, and heavy cream, and decided I regretted my decision less. After adding in honey, Nilla wafers, and liquid nitrogen, I had fully unregretted my decision.

It was surprisingly good! (well, surprising to other people at least; I had full trust in my creation. ignore the part where I regretted all my decisions). The mayonnaise lent it a very distinctive salty flavor, and many campers who tried it didn’t even suspect there was mayonnaise in it. Rating: 55555555/5.
Keti and I with our (well, I don’t think she wants credit for it, so maybe I will say my) mayonnaise creation.
Previous
 
Next

However, I did hear that people who ate the concoction after it had melted had less of a good time; apparently without the coldness you could taste the mayonnaise fully. 

The next flavor was lemon, of which I only remembered to take a picture after it was almost entirely eaten. 

Those were lemon chunks floating in there! Frozen lemon chunks are pretty good. Rating: 4.5/5
The mist is so cool… (I think that yellow thing is a bag of lemons lying on the floor).
We had to prop open a door to the building to get an extension cord in for the electric mixer, so this is what we used for a doorstop. It was expired anyway, so this is probably the most useful it could have been.
Previous
 
Next

The last flavor for the day was Apple, for which we cut up a lot of apples, poured in applesauce, and added honey, Nilla wafers, and cinnamon to top it off. This was also an incredibly good flavor that I seem to not have a photo of :( The fresh apples were very crisp and the ice cream had a very refreshing flavor. 

~~~~~~Week 3~~~~~

Unfortunately, LN2 was cancelled because of rain :( However, we did a makeup LN2 the next Monday, where we had:

Watermelon! Literally just frozen watermelon. Rating: 5/5
Lychee–we poured in two cans of lychee, and it turned out AMAZING. By far my favorite uncursed flavor! It also turns out that there’s a cool reaction when the liquid nitrogen hits the lychee liquid–it was foaming all over the place and looked very cool. Rating: 10/5
Seaweed. Just kidding, it’s matcha, but had a convincing enough color that I could tell people it was seaweed. It was really good, I put in too much matcha (there were still undissolved clumps of matcha floating around…) Rating: 4/5
Previous
 
Next

~~~Week 4~~~

For our second to last week, we had the following flavors:

Cherry! This was our vegan flavor, and was basically just fresh cherries plus oat milk plus liquid nitrogen. It was very good; completely worth the two hours I spent the prior evening pitting cherries. 

Cherry oat milk! The fresh cherries in it paired very well with the oat milk. Rating: 5/5

Mango! This one consisted of heavy cream, half and half, mango extract, and fresh mangos. Except the fresh mangos were also very unripe mangos, and so were very stringy–we tried to cut one, and then gave up. 

The mango extract (which I didn’t know existed before) was very good at doing its job and making things taste like mango. Rating: 5/5

Next up was Sugar Cone, which was originally supposed to be Caramel Cone, but we didn’t have time to make caramel. Since we had lots of honey left over from last week’s honey flavor, we drizzled honey into a cream base and added some sugar cones! Usually we serve ice cream in mini paper cups, but for this flavor we offered a cone option (though it doesn’t work as well for liquid nitrogen ice cream as it does for normal ice cream–LN2 ice cream melts extremely fast, so often you’d be left with just a puddle in a cone, which doesn’t look as aesthetic).

Crushing up the cones in the bowl was extremely satisfying. Rating: 5/5.

All of our flavors this week so far were really good, which is how you know that none of the ideas were mine. In exchange for the good flavors, I was allowed to make two experimental flavors.

The first experimental flavor was Avocado, which we made using fresh avocados (mashed up), condensed milk, cream base, and a spritz of lemon. Keti also had the idea of buying tortilla chips to give to people in lieu of spoons, which was the most brilliant idea ever. 

The ice cream itself shattered my expectations–it was actually really good. The avocado gave the ice cream a lot of creaminess, but didn’t taste weird at all because of the condensed milk we added. Condensed milk is actually such a magic ingredient–it has turned all the cursed flavors we’ve done so far into pretty good flavors. I do kind of wish we had discovered it earlier; it’s a really good substitute for sugar. 

Tortilla chip dipped in avocado ice cream :) the sweet and salty flavors balance out quite well, surprisingly. Rating: 5/5

Our last experimental flavor was supposed to be French Onion Soup Ingredients, but we (un?)fortunately ran out of liquid nitrogen right before, so we could not actually make it. I was mildly disappointed; I had stayed up from 7pm to 1am the previous night attempting to make French Onion Soup . It should not have taken 6 hours. It took 6 hours because I, being a certified Seasoning Hater™ when I cook normally, had not realized that salt was required and not just optional for the onions to caramelize–so they never did (that’s why we were going to call it “French Onion Soup Ingredients” instead of “French Onion Soup”, because it was never actually French Onion Soup :().

The uncaramelized onion soup. Still pretty good, even though it wasn’t frozen in the form of ice cream! Rating: 4/5

~~~Week 5~~~

We did our last LN2 making during Campus Beach Day, a field trip that happened because the weather forecast lied to us. We were originally going to have a real beach day at a real beach, but the weather forecast said it would rain, so it was instead cancelled, and backup field trips to watch Mean Girls at a local cinema and play laser tag were hastily organized. However, when the day came, there was not a cloud in the sky. In fact, it was the best possible weather it could have been for a Beach Day. Since it was then too late to reorganize a Beach Day field trip to a real beach, Beach Day became instead Campus Beach Day, where the lake was replaced with kiddie pools, and the ice cream truck was replaced with liquid nitrogen ice cream.

This week’s flavors were very fruity and summery (because I guess I was in the mood for fruit when we went grocery shopping the hour before). 

Flavor 1: Pear! We got canned pears, put them in the food processor, and then poured liquid nitrogen on it. It turned out just what you’d expect frozen canned pear to taste like; we didn’t add any cream base to it.

I didn’t get a good photo of it before it was all eaten… Rating: 4/5

Flavor 2: Lumpy. At the beginning of camp, a petition was signed to make “Lumpy the Lizard”, a green lizard, the official mascot of camp. He was the mascot for a happy 4.5 weeks, that is, before we ate him. Just kidding! This was actually kiwi flavor. We got a bunch of kiwis and tried to cut them, but quickly discovered that they were quite unripe and hard to cut. Fortunately, the food processor came in handy. The result was this spectacularly lumpy flavor: 

Even though this one had cream base to dilute it, it was still very sour (but a good kind of sour!). Rating: 4.5/5

Flavor 3: Coffee Caramel. Our last flavor this week (and last one for all of camp, even though we didn’t know it then) was made using caramel sauce, instant coffee powder, and a cream base:

I usually don’t like coffee…but this flavor made me change my opinion on it. Rating: 5/5.

After all the campers have had ice cream, there’s usually some melted ice cream left in the bowl. We have a tradition where one of us would pour the remnants of the ice cream straight from the bowl into the other’s mouth. I don’t think I ever had this done to me, partly because my appetite is so done with ice cream by the time that we finish, and partly because of reasons that you will see >:) So, the unlucky victim, uh, I mean recipient of the melted coffee ice cream was Keti. 

In my defense, I was pouring straight and it was the liquid that veered off course at the last moment (you know, you can never trust the direction of gravity). 

Moments after disaster…
She’s so done with me… no, but actually, Keti was the most patient LN2 JC ever–after a whole month of flavors like carrot and pickles and hot sauce and mayonnaise, she still had so much excitement for ice cream.
Previous
 
Next

Ellie’s blog had a really heartfelt conclusion about her feelings of Mathcamp that I on the whole mostly share–but as per my own rules, I’m not allowed to write anything that’s not related to liquid nitrogen in this blog (…maybe in a future blog >:)) So I’ll say this: for me, Mathcamp is like Liquid Nitrogen. It’s pretty cool!

A roiling fog covers the ground… Rating: 3/5. Doesn’t really taste like anything.

Title: don’t build the torment nexus--and other such cliche advice for frosh
Author: Anika H.
Article Content:
After 4 years of undergrad at MIT, I’m back for an MEng (our engineering masters program) and I feel ancient. I first stepped foot on campus in 2022, and now there are class of 30’s. By the time they graduate I’ll be practically prehistoric. Being old doesn’t automatically make you wise, but I’d like to think I have a little bit of wisdom to share. Note that this is mostly train of thought, so these tips are in no particular order. Also I haven’t had time to draw much, so you guys get frogs doodles instead.

american bullfrogs are the largest species of frog in north america and will eat anything that fits in their mouths.

 

dumb questions

While I think you should ask questions all four years of college, you should especially ask a lot freshman year. You guys are young adults, mature enough to live independently on your own for the first time. But at the same time, the rest of us who’ve already experienced MIT for at least a year think you guys are little babies. Like not in the derogatory way; we think you will be experiencing a lot of firsts and will benefit from support to get used to college.

Which means if you have any amount of social anxiety, you should ask as many dumb questions as you can while it’s still socially acceptable. I swear it will be so much less embarrassing asking something when no one expects you to know anything, than when you’re a senior googling basic concepts before an interview. As important as it is to know how to self learn, it’s a lot more efficient asking someone directly.

Foundational knowledge is so very important. It doesn’t matter if you learned it in highschool and forgot, and it doesn’t matter if all your friends know it already. Ask everything you need to properly learn. It’s infinitely worse to be sitting in an advanced class confused about a new concept because it builds on something you never properly learned (I’m speaking from experience, don’t be like me).

Lastly, your lecturers and professors are generally chill. In grade school, teachers would shame you for asking them to repeat something because you weren’t paying attention. But since most professors here are normal reasonable people, they’ll answer anything for you and the handful of other students in the room that probably have the same question. It won’t bother them to repeat one slide out of the 50 they run through that day. However, if you’re still too nervous to ask the professor, ask your neighbor. If they know it, your question is answered. If they don’t, chances are you’re asking a good question that other people also need answered so you can raise your hand confidently.

red eyed tree frogs will open their eyes suddenly to scare away predators.

sucking

As many of you new frosh get thrown into the deep end for the very first time, many of you will fail tests, drop classes, and flounder for dear life. And even more of you, regardless of whether you struggle, will get imposter syndrome. I have it, my friends have it, and the route setters at the MIT Walker climbing gym certainly have it because the difficulty of the routes are several times harder than what it’s rated as. (The ratings are bullshit and the V1s are at least V3s.)

You will suck. And you will feel like you suck. And it might take several years to stop feeling like you suck.

People come to MIT from different backgrounds with vastly different skillsets. I sat in lecture on the first day of Intro to Circuits barely knowing what an op-amp was, and elsewhere in the room, someone had already built a working computer from scratch in high school. You’re all here in the same place not because you know the same things or because you’re all equally genius, but because you have shown the potential to make the best use of MIT’s resources.

“Dude, sucking at something is the first step towards being sorta good at something” – Jake the Dog from Adventure Time

Don’t hinge your self worth to how good you are at a skill. It took me a long time to start to unlearn that from my upbringing. It’s difficult to get rid of that thought completely, so I instead I tried to attach myself to the depth of my passion for engineering and learning. How can you truly say you love a subject until you fail over and over again and keep coming back for more?

Also, don’t compare yourself to people around you if you can help it. It gets 10 times worse at a place like MIT where everyone is cracked. I don’t have any good solutions for this one yet cause I’m still working on it :p

Very recently, even after three full years of knowing how to use test equipment, I forgot to put on an attenuator and broke a 400 dollar NanoVNA. Radio Society added me to the list of value in broken equipment we have cost. The funniest thing is that the people at the top of that leaderboard are some of the best electrical engineers I know. They’ve spent enough time learning to accidentally fry projects and blow things up.

And based off of Radio Society at least, the more mistakes you make, the more you learn from them, the more competent you become.

because desert rain frogs are so rotund, they can’t hop and can only waddle. their screams sound like dog squeaky toys.

social skills

Make friends! make pset buddies! Don’t make enemies even if you’re going for a rival’s to lovers thing which I promise works a lot better in fiction than in real life. You are a wee frosh with light in your eyes, and you can literally ask to sit down at any table in a dining hall, and chances are people will be happy to talk to you for the duration of your half-hour meal. It’s also fine if you just don’t click with someone. Aim to be good acquaintances, and try your chances elsewhere. On a campus with 4000 students you’re bound to find a friend.

While it’s much easier to make friends with your fellow frosh, try to make friends with upperclassmen as well. They know when all the best parties and where all the free food events are. They know which classes are fun, and which ones will drown you in labs. Upperclassmen tend to be a little more tired and cynical than your average froshling, but they have valuable experiences, and are usually more than willing to talk to you in exchange for a few of your extra dining swipes.

One thing I’m sure you’ve all been told if to build a good relationship with your TAs and professors. Many of you will try to do that by going up to the professor after class, introducing yourself, and asking a question about the class content. While this certainly won’t hurt, there are 20 other students trying to do the same exact thing, and 15 minutes later, your poor professor kinda just wants to go home. What you should do instead is to make a consistent effort to show up and engage with the class. Throughout the semester, attendance will slowly dwindle to 1/4 to 1/2 of the lecture hall (unless it’s a HASS class with mandatory attendance). If you continue asking questions in office hours and on piazza and showing up to lecture, you’ll be making a much better impression.

surinam toads embed fertilized eggs into their backs and hatch our fully formed froglets from their backs.

some other tidbits

Don’t use LLMs to write your essays and psets. It can be a useful tool to check answers and review course material, but using it to avoid work and speed through a class defeats the point of taking the class. Your psets have a lot more value in your brain than it does in ChatGPT’s database. Don’t let Sam Altman steal your tuition.

Try not to take classes that use LLMs to generate course material. I’m unfortunately starting to hear about classes with AI generated textbooks, syllabuses, and nonsensical problems, and I’m also starting to hear that those classes are going terribly. If it is a major requirement, try your best to petition out of it.

If you have the energy, join clubs, get involved with campus events and politics, try activism, or if you’re a grad student, join the union. College is one of the best places to start learning how to practice autonomy and expressing yourself. As a student, your voice matters more than you think.

Don’t get blackout drunk at your first party, but if you’re there and you see someone passed out or vomiting a lot, you should call for help. First of all, this is common sense, but also MIT’s Good Samaritan policy will protect you from getting in trouble even if you are not supposed to be there.

Ever heard of the November Rule? Frosh should ideally not be dating anyone until November 1st. Build yourself a friend group and support system of other people. And please please do not date your upperclassmen this early. Their friend group will inevitably become your friend group, and when you break up, they will take their friends and you will have only the few acquaintances you met in Calc class because you didn’t have the opportunity to make your own circle.

If, against your best judgement, you break the November Rule and end up sad or generally do not have anyone’s shoulder to cry on for any reason, or have a social conflict or anything you need to talk about, talk to your GRA. It is in fact their job to help you and direct you to other resources.

Use s^3, also known as Student Support Services. They will help you with most student life related things, but the majority of people go to them for support on assignment extensions. If you get sick or injured or need to move an exam date because of a conference, you should go visit s^3. They also give extensions for mental health reasons but usually won’t budge unless it’s very very severe. However, a common cold usually doesn’t take that much bargaining. These last two sentences are completely unrelated and I do not condone lying to s^3.

In general, exercise common sense. you can be a little bit stupid but don’t be too stupid.

and most importantly…

budgetts frogs have huge mouths that take up a third of their bodies.

be a good person.

before you are student at MIT, you are a person living among other people in this world, and you will live among people for the rest of your life. Be kind to others, be kind to yourself, and assume ignorance before malice. It’s fine to dislike people and argue, but don’t harrass or antagonize people, don’t steal other people’s stuff or food out the communal fridge, dont gloat about how easy a class is in front of someone who’s obviously struggling, slow down your e-scooter when there’s a lot of foot traffic around, etc etc.

And for the love of all that is good, PLEASE don’t make the torment nexus or the newest missile guidance system or a health insurance claim denial algorithm with higher profit margins. Yes, the job market is really bad right now, but I promise you can get an equally high paying job doing something less terrible with an MIT education.

the torment nexus, for those who don’t get the reference

You have an opportunity to study at the best technical school in the world, and I sincerely hope that you can use your newfound knowledge and community to make our shitty world a better place.

newly discovered in 2021, the zombie frog got its name because the researchers looked like zombies digging them out of the ground. they look like overweight muppets.

 

Stay safe and good luck with your first semester!

Title: my “first” “week” of “classes” at mit--or, discovering course 1 through a first-year pre-orientation program
Author: Suzuko O.
Article Content:
despite getting to campus over two weeks ago, my classes only started today. ??? what was i doing for all this time ???⁠01

there’s a bunch of things – resident exploration (REX), floor rush, frat rush – that all seem to mix into each other, but at least for the first four days i have a nice clean answer:

i was doing my fpop!

what’s an fpop?

glad you asked! fpop (pronounced eff-pop)⁠02 stands for “freshman pre-orientation program”.

…but what does that mean? is a question a lot of people have asked (namely, my parents). 

i think my brain is rotted

i am going to take a somewhat circuitous route to try to explain. here’s my vague understanding of how all of this pre-school school stuff came to be

the base case is that kids come to school and immediately start class
mit (and other colleges) realized that this is a Lot to expect of freshmen, who are probably not used to being on campus or to being away from home or to like. cooking and doing laundry
yay! orientation! to orientate⁠03 the kids!
hey, wait… what if we wanted to PRE-orient the kids? that way they can get around orientation better!
this seems like a great time to insert an Educational Opportunity⁠04

to get to the point, an fpop generally is themed around one of the courses (fancy mit word for majors) at mit. some of the ones my friends did include deaps (discover earth and planetary sciences, which took a daytrip to new hampshire), dns (discover nuclear science, which made my friend consider switching her major from physics), and discover physics (who got forced to go to an art museum because of rain). 

the one i did was called dc1, which stands for discover course 1. unfortunately the average mit prefrosh⁠05 has no clue what course 1 is, so i always had to postface by saying “…which is civil and environmental engineering” (cee). usually after i said that people’s stares of abject confusion would clear into stares of slightly hopeful confusion.

why i chose dc1

one mandatory question that you will inevitably be asked approximately five hundred billion times is “what course are you thinking of studying?” indeed, i was asked this by possibly every prefrosh and upperclassman involved in my fpop. it was always kind of awkward because my response to “are you thinking of studying course 1?” was always “uhh probably not i’m thinking 20 (bioengineering) or maybe 7 (biology)”, and then people would be like “…so why are you here” 

my answer to this is a mix of the following factors, in descending order:

what i want to do with biology is find applications in environment/climate/sustainability, so i thought civil and environmental engineering would be a cool other perspective on this
this fpop was free⁠06
it’s small (only 15 kids, compared to discover physics which was like 30) which i thought was better and less overwhelming
they promised trips around cambridge

during the (very chill) application process, i had to write a few essays justifying why i was interested in dc1,⁠07 and why they should choose me and whatnot. luckily i ended up with my first choice! yippee!

day one: move-in + barbecue

one perk of doing an fpop is that you get to move in a few days early. my move-in date was august 25th, compared to all non-fpoppers, who moved in on august 29th. this is not a super big difference but i think it makes it calmer which was somewhat nice. 

i spent most of the 25th moving in. my mom came to boston (yay!) so she helped me move all my bags from the hotel we were staying in to my room. east campus has a weird system where the room we initially stay in (in mit lingo, where we’re “temped”) is highly unlikely to be our permanent room, so i was told to try to unpack as little as possible – which, of course, sounds great! i was also really sleepy because i had stayed up till 3am the night before…solving sudoku… so basically i did some basic unpacking and then immediately took a two hour nap. 

at some point during my nap, my friend eddy ’30 knocked on my door to deliver…

A LARGE SHARK

BIG SHARK (pillow for scale)

this guy has lived on my bed for the past two weeks. he takes up a third of the available space on my bed. he makes it vaguely inconvenient to sleep on my bed. BUT I LOVE HIM (name is undecided but some names floating around include stockfish and crouton). eternal thanks to eddy for dragging this adorable guy across the country to his new home C:

after i woke up from my nap i basically ran around the campus meeting up with friends. or i guess before that i went to the stud⁠08 to eat some leftover pizza with my mom, where i also ran into SO MANY PEOPLE, and then i ran around campus to see friends. first i went to burton-conner (usually just called bc) to meet my friend scarlet ‘30 and kind of awkwardly watch as she unpacked her suitcase. a bit later, she and i went to new house to try to jumpscare our friend freddy ‘30!! freddy is not french but is now french due to living in french house, one of the 9 halls in new house. 

all in all good times. 

the first required meeting of the day was a fpop barbecue at 5, where we would all get into our fpop groups for the first time and meet our mentors and whatnot.⁠09 i honestly don’t remember very much about this except that we had to wait a long time for food and that i tried to remember people’s names, but it was pretty hard… even with only ~15 other names to learn…

i almost definitely hung out with friends after the barbecue but i have no clue who, or what we did, so uhh idk 💀 let’s timeskip to the next day!

day two: egg drop and starting the project

we started off day two with an 8:30 pancake breakfast (yay!) in building 1, which is at the very edge of the “main group” of buildings. i’m not sure if i showed up to this breakfast on time – my assumption is that i probably didn’t because i was still “jet lagged” (my favorite excuse for not going to sleep at a reasonable time). but eventually i did go to breakfast and i did eat pancakes and i started to get to know my fellow fpoppers! i think on this day they had ran out of normal-height chairs at one of the tables so i sat on a tall chair instead, like a giraffe in a pack of horses. 

from 9:15 we had an introduction to the fpop program and to our academic staff. we went through the room and introduced ourselves (again, i’m glad that we were in a small fpop – i imagine that in a larger one introductions either took forever or just did not happen in the same depth). we also got divided into our group project (more on this later) groups based on the tried and true method of assign everyone a number. 

from 10:30 to 12, in our newly assigned groups, we had a scavenger hunt of campus! we used some weird app that made us take pictures of ourselves at 8 different locations, including the banana lounge, the course 1 academic office, the parsons building (where all the course 1 laboratories are located), the tunnels under some of the eastern buildings,⁠10 the walker memorial, and some other sites. while we walked around, i got to know my teammates from maryland, washington state, and indonesia, who were interested in studying courses as varied as 18 (math) and 10 (chemical engineering). approximately an hour after we started, we returned to our homebase and found that we had finished third. (later on when i wasn’t really paying attention, someone told our team that we won something, but i couldn’t make out what that something specifically was. but by process of elimination i think it might’ve been this scavenger hunt?)

from 12 we had a big lunch with civil and environmental engineering professor tal cohen and her lab. this was pretty cool because her lab does like all sorts of stuff – you would expect that perhaps a cee lab would do mainly mechanical/structural type things, and this lab did have some projects in this realm (for example, i think there was someone working on car crash impacts) but there were also people in the lab doing wet-lab experiments on mice hearts (or possibly brains… my memory really isn’t good huh), which piqued my interest because I LIKE biology!! among the six different projects or so that we were introduced to, the professor explained that the unifying theme is the idea of mechanics; more broadly, i understood that the civil and environmental engineering department is more expansive than i had previously thought.⁠11

also, this lunch had winston in attendance. winston is the course 1 emotional support dog. he is a silly little pug and he is adorable. there was time in the lunch to ask questions to all the phd students, but i spent all of my time talking to winston. he is soooooo cute i think he can be found in the c1 academic office on wednesdays? i should try to find him again

look at him he is so cute

after lunch, we went downstairs to the building 1 basement, into a room with a bunch of hydraulic presses. if you’ve ever seen youtube videos where people crush random stuff with a big metal machine, it’s like that – but the ones in this basement are like REALLY BIG, to where the units of force that our instructor steve rudolph used to describe them was in terms of elephants (or maybe thousands of elephants??? actually that sounds ridiculous). we looked at how engineered defects in metal cylinders can cause consistent patterns of deformation, and later we cracked an egg to see how the peak force resisted changed based on the end that it was cracked at.⁠12

this thing lives in my backpack now i should probably take it out

now, building off this eggcellent information, we moved on to our first hands-on module of the week! in elementary school science demonstration-style, our task was to make a thing that could protect an egg from cracking after being dropped from the second floor of lobby 7. our materials were limited to toothpicks, 6 popsicle sticks, and a roll of twine (also hot glue for adhesive purposes). not only were we competing (friendly-ly) against one another, we were also fighting a team with ALL grad students and also a few teams with like elementary school kids. so you know, a variety of strong opposition

after taking a brief nap, we started construction. to be honest no one in our group was very confident about anything, so we spent the first half of our allotted 40 minutes just kind of doing stuff. my idea was to cover our egg in twine, then attach toothpicks radially outward to act as shock absorbers, so i started twining our egg – but halfway through we decided to build some sort of toothpick parallelopiped thing, which we then wrapped in a bunch of twine. (during the brief “explain your design” part we kind of just said “yeah we don’t know we just did whatever”)

then it was time to drop the egg! our egg broke :( but the grad students’ egg did not!⁠13 i think everyone else’s may have? i’m not sure – i kind of got distracted by some friends in the discover physics fpop, who were also doing some sort of egg drop in the same location.

now, around 4pm, it was finally time to start our group project… which i was somewhat apprehensive about. like many people, i am not the hugest fan of group projects… but open mind! our group chose a problem on mit’s campus to tackle from the categories of energy, waste, transportation, or building design. after some discussion, we decided to focus on energy, with a team member proposing the idea of installing piezoelectric tiles on the tennis courts in order to generate the electricity needed to keep the lights on.⁠14

we had some free time, so two of my group members and i decided to try to work out in the Z (short for the zesiger center, mit’s main recreation/sports center). unfortunately they said we needed physical id and wouldn’t let us in… boo! so instead we walked allllll the way to next house,⁠15 where jesslyn showed us her room. then we walked back to killian court,⁠16 where the rest of our fpop was playing mafia. i enjoyed pizza and the ambience of being outside

that was it for our scheduled second-day fpop activities :) 

day three: wind + more group project

i showed up like 10 minutes before breakfast ended (again… not the earliest of sleep times…) and then it was time for activities!

we first had 30 minutes of work time on our projects. here, we decided to do a hard pivot into a much less serious direction. as we joked around about various ridiculous ideas, we came to the idea of harnessing the power of living things to solve the energy crisis. more specifically, we saw a vision of a world where mit’s rodent problem (generally a scourge) became one of our strengths⁠17

this idea, because of its absolute whimsy and silliness, immediately made me much more enthusiastic about our project. unfortunately we were no able to work on it right then and there because we had more activities. BOOOO just kidding

our first speaker this day was jared berezin, the manager of cee’s version of the communication lab. i really care about science communication (especially through writing, which is one of the reasons i wanted to be a blogger in the first place!) so i think this is pretty awesome – it turns out that every engineering department has its own subdivision, which have grad students who are trained in conveying science better, who we as undergraduates can reach out to and get help from (whether it be making slides or writing papers or whatever). his presentation was quite well done and it made me want to get involved in the comm labs – i am not sure if they have many opportunities for undergraduates to contribute, but this is something to look into in the future. 

ironically, the presentation that followed was not uhhh particularly communicated quite well… but it was still cool! two grad students from the zardini group came in to present their work on game theory in transportation systems, and afterwards we played an interactive game where our various groups played the parts of different entities in the transportation sector (for example, rent-a-bike companies, public transit authorities, or autonomous vehicle companies.)⁠18 to be honest i do not know what i took away from this activity, but you know that’s okay.

after a quick chipotle lunch where we had wayyy too many chips,⁠19 it was time for another module. first, two grad students from the howland lab presented about their work, which generally centers on the computational modeling of wind flow. one thing that they talked about was a diagram of something navier-stokes-related, which is a bit of fun foreshadowing given what has since transpired.⁠20 then we made our own miniturbines out of foam and paper! this was actually quite fun. i am a big fan of scissors and glue and little hand crafts so i thought this was great.

spinni

we continued to work on our slides, researching and editing, and in our group’s case, going to metropolis.⁠21 here, a kind mentor helped us slightly edit a treadmill model and print it using one of the many 3d printers that compose a makeshift wall in the space. 

TREADMILL!

the day ended as we had an fpop dinner while watching wall-e. this was my first time actually watching wall-e⁠22 and it was quite striking for me. as a lot of my friends can attest, i think the first 10 minutes of wall-e is among the best examples of like environmental storytelling and body language that i have seen – i felt so much empathy towards this little robot guy living in a world of vastly different scale. i think it was super well done. i think the rest of the movie is like good but not nearly as good as the first ten minutes are, but it was fun!

to round off the day, i crossed the harvard bridge⁠23 with a few fpop friends to go to chicha san chen, a very fancy boba shop (like very very fancy) on the recommendation of one of our fpop mentors. i ended up not buying a drink that day because i was super full,⁠24 but it was nice to walk across the bridge as the sun went down. i really like the charles river :)  

so pretty

day four: final presentations and ice cream!

on day four, i once again woke up just early enough to catch the end of breakfast. from 9:30 to 11:45, we finished and fine-tuned our presentation slides, talking over some of the transitions and doing a practice run in front of our mentor suhaila ‘28. finally at 12, it was time for our presentations!

in the audience was everyone in the fpop, alongside some of the grad students that had spoken to us earlier in the week and some New Fun grad students! yay. while eating my sandwich, my group watched as the other three groups presented their work. a brief recap:

one group presented about an idea for a small electrical waste disposal facility to be located on mit’s campus, to reduce the need for offloading to outside facilities and to aid in the recovery of valuable metals. they made a 3d model out of cardboard for what the facility could look like
another group presented an idea for making bus stops more friendly, both to people and the environment. they proposed curvy solar panels for the ceiling (to make rain fall off easier) and uhh something whose name i forgot, but basically amounts to water-absorbent green spaces on the curb. they had a live demonstration that i thought was awesome – they had a 3d model of a bus stop with sponges underneath, and demonstrated the ability of the sponges to absorb by dripping water over it
the last group presented about green roofs! they proposed adding these to different mit dorms, exploring feasibility and cost. i thought it was very well done.

finally, it was our turn. in lieu of explaining our presentation, i think i will just insert the slideshow. have fun scrolling through (and guessing at what we said)!

it was not particularly stressful and i think the audience laughed more than i feared they would. especially since the other three presentations were quite serious, i think ours was a nice change of pace – it inspired a lot of funny questions that were, you know, natural extensions of the work we did. 

we had some free time until like 5, when we had a (free!) dinner from naco taco, a mexican restaurant nearby (maybe a 10 minute walk from lobby 7?) i spent 18 dollars of someone else’s money on a shrimp burrito, which i thought was passable but not particularly. value-worthy.⁠25 here, we smuggled around a card that all of us signed for our mentors thanking them for all their work. afterwards we went to toscanini’s⁠26 where i got mango sticky rice ice cream! highly recommend. 

that marked the end of my fpop experience :) it was a fun time!

what next? 

the next week and a half or so was a whirlwind: first we had resident exploration (like a repeat of cpw, where all the dorms run fun events and gives free food), then orientation, then floor rush (where i finally got to choose a floor on east campus to call home!), then frat rush (which i didn’t think i would do, but got reasonably invested in). now classes have started so i’m hoping that things seem to settle down a bit more. 

but to answer (or, i guess, ask) this question more thematically: how will my experience with the dc1 fpop weave into the rest of my time at mit? 

well, as i walk the halls of mit to get to 5.112 (my chem class) or 18.03 (differential equations), i see people from my fpop and wave to them. a lot of dc1 fpoppers are in terrascope, my first-year learning community centered on environment and sustainability, which has at its core a group project where we work to find solutions for an environmental problem.⁠27

i think terrascope is the spiritual successor to the dc1 fpop in my mind: both focus on group projects on environmental problems. i also think that i am not particularly good at group projects, or working on big, nebulous problems, or self-directing and organizing; i think this will make terrascope kind of frustrating for me, but also really good for my character growth. you’ll probably hear more from me about terrascope soon?

but i guess to end on topic: tl;dr my fpop was fun! i’m glad i did it C:

Title: Classes I’m Taking My Freshman Fall!(And Other Things Too)--can you believe they're letting me do one of these?
Author: Leya E.
Article Content:
It’s 2020. I am sitting in my room reading blogs from MIT students about classes they’ve taken.

It is 2023. I am sitting in my room reading blogs from MIT students about classes they’ve taken.

It is December 2025. I am sitting in my room, crying after getting my admissions decision, and reading blogs from MIT students about classes they’ve taken.

It is September 2026. I am sitting in my dorm room, writing a blog about the classes I’m taking.

It really doesn’t feel real. Even as I’m sitting here, writing this, I still can’t quite believe I’m actually here.

I still slightly think this whole blogger thing is a lie and that nobody will actually read this except me.

But in case someone is actually reading this, I felt that it was only right to start my blogger career with my favorite type of post: one about my classes!

I’m taking 5 classes this semester, which is kind of a heavy workload, especially when one of those classes is estimated to take 15 hours a week. But we’ll get to that.

I’m taking:

ES.1802 – Multivariable Calculus

ES.5111 – Principles of Chemical Science

8.012 – Classical Mechanics

6.1903 – Introduction to C and Assembly

21L.032 – Afrofuturism, Magical Realism, and Other Otherwise Worlds

ES.1802

Let’s start with my ESG classes. ESG stands for Experimental Study Group, and it’s one of a couple of first year learning communities that first-years can apply to. One of the main appeals of ESG is having classes in small group formats that are more hands-on than large lecture-style mainstream classes.⁠01 Another thing about ESG classes compared to mainstream is that, at least for the ones I’m taking, they meet every day and are all attendance required. ES.1802 is multivariable calculus, like mainstream 18.02, except my class has 12 people instead of like 500. I really like the way that things are explained in this class, like the very cool derivations of the dot product and cross product we did. However, I hadn’t seen multivariable calculus material before arriving at MIT, so it’s going to be a lot more new to me than to some of my classmates. We’re starting pretty slow though, so I think I’ll be able to catch up.

ES.5111

This is normal chemistry, just like mainstream 5.111. I actually wanted to take 3.091⁠02 instead but it didn’t fit in my schedule :(. It’s fine though, this class is still very cool! I kind of forgot just how interesting chemistry is, at least when you’re not agonizing over sig figs which our first PSET is focused on. The first week, we went through some history of how our understanding of the atom has evolved, which leads us to how quantum mechanics was created! This is very exciting to me as a physics nerd. Speaking of…

8.012

At MIT, everyone has to take some version of Physics I⁠03 unless you test out of it with AP scores. I did not. Another way to get out of it is to pass the 8.01 ASE. I did not. But because I have a lot of belief in myself, I decided to take the harder version of 8.01! 8.012 is designed for people who have above-average math skills and above-average baseline physics knowledge. I’d like to think I have these things, and I also discussed it with my advisor⁠04 , and we agreed that I could try 8.012 and potentially drop to ES.801 if it got too hard. This class is also a lot more work than 8.01. This is the class that is projected to take 15 hours a week. I don’t think that it will take that long for me, but crowdsourcing opinions is always a good idea to sanity check your schedule. I reviewed both the textbook and the syllabus⁠05 and so far I believe that I can do it. The class moves at a faster pace than 8.01, which is what I mainly wanted since I thought that 8.01 would be too much review for me. It also covers a couple more topics, which is also something I wanted. Right now I think I’ve made the right choice, but I’ll let you know in a few weeks if I end up changing my mind. The first class was interrupted by a humanoid robot, so that was pretty cool I guess.⁠06

He waved at us.

6.1903

This class is, like it says from the title, an introduction to low-level programming in C and Assembly. I’m pretty sure this is the first time it’s been taught over a full semester instead of 6 weeks, so I feel like the workload might seem less intense than previous years, but you never know. This class has “optional” recitations which is pretty cool, but I do also have a mandatory lab from 7:30pm to 9:30pm. So. At the very least it’s not every week. We also get a cool little lab kit with a cheap little microcontroller! I love microcontrollers. They’re like computers but…micro…

21L.032

I am SO EXCITED for this class! Like guys you don’t understand the first thing I did when I was admitted was make a list of classes I wanted to take and this one was literally FIRST ON MY LIST! I was so happy when I got the email saying I got in.⁠07 We are watching 8 films this semester including Sinners, Nope, Black Panther, and Encanto, and reading a lot of books and short stories, starting with Toni Morrison’s Beloved. This might be my favorite class ever just from the syllabus. I also really appreciated the discussion we had on the first day, because it feels like it’s been a long time since I’ve been in a humanities class where everyone was actually invested in having thoughtful discussions about the material. It’s nice to find a space like that at MIT, especially considering the amount of technical classes I’m taking.

 

So yeah! That’s my freshman fall in a nutshell. I am also of course, sidequesting as best as possible, since it’s PNR⁠08 so like nothing matters if you think about it…⁠09 So here’s a list of other things I have done so far:

Larping but like actually

I went to the Assassin’s Guild’s⁠10 patrol game last saturday to fulfill my childhood dreams of shooting people with nerf guns. I cannot say that I was very good at it. I also got roped into applying to their next actual role-playing game, which is about potatoes I think. I’m so excited.

Being too close to fire

After the patrol game I walked with the other patrol players to the MIT Spinning Arts club’s firespinning show! It was the first time I’d ever seen firespinning and we were also in the front row so that was slightly unnerving. However, watching firespinning is awesome and probably the closest thing to witnessing real life magic.

Learning what Ultrakill is

I went to a DAAMIT⁠11 meeting and through various conversations tangentially related to digital art learned what Ultrakill was.⁠12 Fun! We also played Gartic Phone⁠13 and learned that all roads lead to Hatsune Miku. Miku dayo!

Singing!

I “auditioned” for Next Sing⁠14 and filled out a form CORRECTLY⁠15 to list what acts I want to be in. One of the options is the Cafeteria Song from My Little Pony Equestria Girls. I NEED to be in the Cafeteria Song from My LIttle Pony Equestria Girls.

Learning About Various Non-Academic Topics

I went to the firestorm event hosted by the Educational Studies Program⁠16 , where people got to host five minute talks about whatever they wanted! I did arrive late and so did not get free food, but did get a very comfortable free shirt. And of course, learned about things such as the dvorak keyboard layout and the fact that Italy can make bad pizza too.

what are they doing in Italy

 

There are other things I’m planning on doing too, like joining Next Haunt just to get the guaranteed run-through of the escape room,⁠17 being part of Next Act⁠18 , joining combat robotics, auditioning for a role in the Shakespeare Ensemble’s production of King Lear, and pretty much anything else on dormspam⁠19 that seems slightly interesting.

I think the point of freshman year is to explore everything, and if you don’t feel awestruck with the amount of possibilities you have at least once, you’re probably not doing it right. I know I can’t do everything, and that the fun I’m having right now probably won’t last,⁠20 but I want to take advantage of the freedom I’ve been given as a newly minted college student and deprived myself of as a high schooler.

Coming to MIT, I feel like I’m finally surrounded by a community of people where I don’t need to hide parts of myself to be accepted.

I am cringe but I am free.

Here’s to the next four years!

Title: morning shrine--early days in senior fall
Author: Veronica P.
Article Content:
this morning i was awake at 6am. on the other end of one of those things i do where i allow myself to fall asleep, once my brain has settled to mush and past it’s point of productivity, and i tell myself that when i wake up early the next morning, i will be clean, shiny, and focused, and do all the work i want to do. in this grey-blue light i am not quite clean, shiny, or focused, but i am renewed and on my way to being those things. the sweat of a sleep well slept is sticking onto my skin, and the weight of my blanket is insisting that i don’t have to be at my meeting until 11:30. why not stay a while?

when i wake up i face the side of my dresser. i’ve taped a sign my friend made when i picked her up from the airport my sophomore year: “HAPPY BDAY VERO <3.” last spring i added, atop the dresser, a box from my roommate that reads, “RONNIE’S 21st!” the idea of these being the first words i read each morning reminds me of a taylor swift lyric. i don’t love it, but i have enough nostalgic sentimentality towards t.s. to know it: “I’m so depressed, I act like it’s my birthdayyyyy every day!” it doesn’t quite apply, at least currently. maybe it can be called a preventative measure.

last spring i also added, to this morning shrine, an award i got from doing well in one of my classes. it is the single most tangible piece of academic validation that i have gotten at this institution, so i cherish it with A+ fridge-magnet levels of pride. for some reason, when i look at it this morning, i think of a conversation i had at 3am this past summer, on a rooftop on beacon st.

in the midst of catch-up, i mentioned that i had just decided to try for grad school, post-MIT. a good friend, the second friend i ever made at this school, overhears and interjects with an exaggerated sigh of relief: “finally.” when prompted, he explained that it was obvious that this was the path for me. any of my “confusion” over these past few years was just fear manifesting: intimidation about straying from my industry-oriented friends, dread at the thought of going for what i truly want and not getting it. it was the “finally” of a reader who had figured out whodunnit by Chapter 2,  finally getting to see the detective piece together that the killer was right there all along. 

i don’t know how much of that friend’s conviction is true. the thought is nice to contemplate, to believe every once in a while. certainly when i am budgeting times to chip away at applications and planning professors to ask for letters of recommendation, it is reassuring to buy into the idea of a true calling. a purpose that exists for each person to uncover from their depths, right there all along. the veil lifting is my litmus test, the indication that i have matured enough to look my calling in the eye and pursue it.

it is nice to believe it is true. words like these instill a confidence, perhaps undue, that i need to make it through the worst parts of this Fall. to push through the weight of my blanket and convince other people, not just myself, that grad school could be a tangible next step for me. not like when i asked my academic advisor, a week ago, if i might not be ready, compelling her to adamantly affirm, “yes, you are.” i take these words as part of my morning shrine, as well, and work on being that affirmation myself.

Title: i’m a sneaky little scavenger--acquiring furniture in the bay area
Author: Allison E.
Article Content:
have you ever wanted to furnish an apartment for as little money as possible? are you a sneaky little scavenger?

hee hee hee ha ha ha

here are some ideas, courtesy of me and my amazing summer roommate grace :D

1.  find furniture on the side of the street

in the words of one of my friends, “welcome to the wonderful wastage of the bay area”! i lived in downtown-ish San Jose this summer and there was SO MUCH FURNITURE ABANDONED ON THE SIDE OF THE ROAD (smth smth college students ig) (seriously i think i found at least 35 pieces of furniture on this one street over 2.5 months, including like 6 couches)

classic ikea malm dresser... almost almost decided to bring this one home
unfortunately my roommate only had a twin futon mattress so we couldn't use this
couches are suspiscious
Previous
 
Next

generally i would not recommend taking mattresses and couches due to potential small evil critter issues. however, metal, plastic, and even wood are less nefarious. i ended up acquiring an entire bed frame and a room divider thingy (i was sleeping in the living room so this was helpful)

genuinely never realized how much a bedframe improves quality of life, and idek why
privacy yay :D
Previous
 
Next

2.  steal cardboard boxes from costco

so uh i did not realize this but there’s a bunch of random table-things that are useful in an apartment. dining room table, desk, nightstand, dresser, etc. etc. that is many items! i did not want to pay for and later get rid of that many items.

solution: STEAL BOXES FROM COSTCO

cardboard boxes from costco are shockingly sturdy objects, AND they come in extremely convenient shapes. the standard cardboard box (rectangular prism) is suboptimal for table use because it’s one convex solid and you can’t put your legs “underneath” the table surface, so instead you must place the box at arms length and eat dinner bent forward in uncomfortable supplication to the cardboard. Costco boxes, on the other hand, are open in the front and provide a convenient place to put your feet and/or other miscellaneous objects! This means they work not only as dinner tables, but as double-tiered nightstands, dresser drawers, and assorted elevated surfaces.

there’s even a little slot at the top where you can put your charger so it doesn’t end up tangled somewhere

 

3.  get yourself a roommate who has family in the area

chairs are kinda hard to acquire without the possibility of also acquiring small evil critter issues, so we borrowed 2 folding lawn chairs from my roommate’s family

these chairs were actually amazingly comfy

4.  make your roommate acquire free stuff from santa clara students

free microwave! and free desk fan thingy! lowkey have not encountered a microwave with a physical windup timer instead of a digit pad, but it was in perfect condition.

highkey SUPER clean, great find by my roommate

5.  what is a trash can? who needs that

all you need are trash bags and a hook (you don’t even need a hook)

[i don’t have a picture but just imagine a large black trash bag hooked to the side of the fridge]

6.  buy a couple things ig

i shelled out for a nice futon mattress to sleep on, a $10 ikea clothesrack, and an $8 rug for shoes. also like $8 for two very sturdy very plastic home depot buckets that turned into footstools, secondary tables, and waterproof surfaces (since all the rest of our surfaces were cardboard 💀)

afterword:

the final product! our living room / my bedroom :D

i have tragically become the stereotype of a true tech bro 😔 BUT i did save a lot of money on furniture so i consider that a win. moral of the story? maybe find summer housing that’s already furnished. but also rent is cheaper if you don’t 🤷
